Every time you double‑click that template file, it generates a new document inheriting all those settings, while the original template remains unchanged. Some universities provide a graduation thesis template as a file. It contains pre‑set formatting and may include automation scripts (e.g., one‑click checking of figure/table numbering). If the file is , Word will prompt you to “Enable Macros” – you need to allow this to use all features. Where to put templates: The default location is . After placing templates there, they appear under “File” → “New” → “Personal”. Word Extended Reading Extended 1: Linking Styles to Table of Contents When generating a table of contents, Word by default only looks for “Heading 1”, “Heading 2”, and “Heading 3”. If you use custom styles (e.g., “Chapter Title”), go to “References” → “Table of Contents” → “Custom Table of Contents” → “Options” to manually assign heading levels. Extended 2: Section Breaks A Section Break is more powerful than a simple page break. After inserting a section break, each section can have its own margins, headers/footers, and page orientation. For example, the preface and table of contents might use Roman numeral page numbers, while the main body uses Arabic numerals. A section break in between makes this possible. How to insert: Layout → Breaks → Next Page (this is a section break). Extended 3: Document Page Colour The “Never change document page colour” setting in Word Options exists precisely because of dark mode. Windows 11’s dark mode affects Office – Word may show black background with white text. However, the actual document background is still white. If someone changes font colours to something light (e.g., light grey) while using dark mode, those colours may become illegible when the document is opened on a white background (as your instructor likely will). Keeping the defaults is safest. Part 2: Excel Excel is a spreadsheet tool for working with data, performing calculations, and creating charts. Many people only type into cells and feel intimidated by formulas. This section covers only what you will actually use during university – no overly complex functions. 2.1 Basic Operations A Cell is the smallest unit in a spreadsheet, identified by its column letter and row number – for example, means column 2, row 3. A Range is a contiguous block of cells, written as the top‑left cell and bottom‑right cell separated by a colon. For example, covers all cells from A1 through C10. Common shortcuts: | Action | Method | |--------|--------| | Select an entire row | Click the row number | | Select an entire column | Click the column letter | | Select the whole sheet | Click the triangle at the top‑left (between A and 1) | | Fill the same content downward | Select the cell, drag the small square at the bottom‑right (fill handle) | | Fill a sequence | Hold while dragging the fill handle (or enter two values so Excel detects the pattern) | | Auto‑fit column width / row height | Double‑click the divider between column letters (or row numbers) | 2.2 Formulas and Functions Formulas begin with . For example, typing into a cell will display after you press Enter. Common functions | Function | Purpose | Example | |----------|---------|---------| | | Adds numbers | | | | Average | | | | Counts numeric cells | | | | Counts non‑empty cells | | | / | Largest / smallest value | | | | Conditional logic | | Important concept: Relative vs Absolute Reference In a formula, is a relative reference. When you drag the formula down, it automatically becomes , , etc. is an absolute reference – it stays the same when dragged. There are also mixed references: (column fixed, row flexible) and (row fixed, column flexible). Press to quickly cycle through these four reference modes. Example: Calculate each sale’s percentage of total sales. Assume sales figures are in and the total is in . The formula for the first row is . The is locked, so when you drag the formula down, the total cell never changes. 2.3 Lookup & Reference Functions This is Excel’s core power: finding data from one table based on a value in another. VLOOKUP (Vertical Lookup) Syntax: Example: You have a student grade table – column A is student ID, column B is name, column C is grade. You want to find the grade for a given ID: F2: the student ID to look for A:C: look within columns A through C (the first column of this range must contain the ID) 3: once found, return the value from the 3rd column of the range (column C, the grade) 0: exact match Important notes: The lookup value must be in the first column of the lookup range only searches left‑to‑right; it cannot return values from columns to the left of the lookup column Always use (or ) for exact match – do not omit it XLOOKUP (Office 365 only) is an improved version that fixes many of ’s limitations. The syntax is simpler, it can look left, and you can specify a custom “not found” message. Syntax: Example: Version differences: Office 2021 and Office 365 support , , , and other new functions Office 2019 and older do not. If you send someone an older‑version Excel file containing , they will see a error INDEX + MATCH (universal, works in all versions) returns the value at a given row and column within a range. finds the position of a value within a list. Together they can perform two‑way lookups. Example: Find a grade based on student name and subject name: 2.4 Text and Date Functions Text functions | Function | Purpose | Example | |----------|---------|---------| | | Takes n characters from the left | → "2024" | | | Takes n characters from the right | | | | Takes middle characters | → "09" | | operator | Concatenates text | | | | Formats numbers or dates | | Date functions | Function | Purpose | Example | |----------|---------|---------| | | Current date | Updates automatically each day | | | Current date and time | | | | Extracts the year | | | | Extracts the month | | | | Extracts the day | | | | Difference between two dates | calculates age | 2.5 Conditional Statistics | Function | Purpose | Example | |----------|---------|---------| | | Counts cells meeting a condition | | | | Sums cells meeting a condition | | | | Averages cells meeting a condition | | 2.6 Pivot Tables A Pivot Table is the most powerful data analysis tool in Excel. With a few clicks, you can generate summary reports from thousands of rows of data. Scenario: You have a school‑wide grade table with columns “Class”, “Student Name”, “Subject”, “Grade” – 5,000 rows total. You want to know the average grade per class, the highest grade per subject, or the distribution of grades by class and subject. A pivot table does this in seconds. Steps: Select the entire data range Click “Insert” → “PivotTable” In the pop‑up, choose “New Worksheet” In the “PivotTable Fields” panel, drag fields into different areas: Rows: what you want to group by (e.g., “Class”) Columns: what you want to cross‑tabulate with (e.g., “Subject”) Values: what you want to calculate (e.g., “Grade”). By default it sums; click “Value Field Settings” to change to “Average” or “Count” 2.7 Creating Charts Select your data → “Insert” → “Chart”. Common types: Column chart: Compare values across categories Line chart: Show trends over time Pie chart: Show proportions of a whole (use with at most 5 slices, otherwise it gets messy) Consider adding titles, data labels, and axis descriptions. Right‑click on the chart to change chart type, colour palette, add trendlines, etc. 2.8 Conditional Formatting Conditional Formatting makes cells automatically change colour based on their values. Select your data → “Home” → “Conditional Formatting”. Useful rules: Highlight cells rules: highlight values above a threshold in red, duplicate values in yellow Colour scales: shade cells from green (high) to red (low) Data bars: draw a bar inside each cell whose length represents the value – no extra space needed Icon sets: use traffic lights or arrows to indicate high/medium/low 2.9 Data Validation Data Validation restricts what can be typed into a cell, preventing errors. Select a cell → “Data” → “Data Validation” → “Settings” → “Allow” choose “List”. In “Source”, type your options separated by commas (e.g., ). That cell now becomes a dropdown menu. Common restrictions: List → dropdown menu Whole number → limit to a range (e.g., 0 to 100) Date → restrict to a date range Text length → limit number of characters (e.g., phone number must be 11 digits) 2.10 Shortcuts | Shortcut | Effect | |----------|--------| | | Jump to the edge of the data region | | | Select the entire contiguous region | | | AutoSum (inserts a SUM formula) | | | Repeat the last action (e.g., repeat inserting a row, repeat formatting) | | | Edit the current cell (instead of double‑clicking) | | | Fill down (copy from the cell above) | | | Fill right | | | Open the Format Cells dialog | | | Turn filters on/off | Excel Extended Reading Extended 1: Function Differences – Office 2021 vs. Office 365 | Function | Office 2021 | Office 365 | Notes | |----------|-------------|------------|-------| | | ✅ | ✅ | Also available in 2021 | | | ❌ | ✅ | 365 only – auto‑filters and returns results | | | ❌ | ✅ | 365 only – sorts automatically | | | ❌ | ✅ | 365 only – extracts unique values | | | ✅ | ✅ | Joins text with a delimiter | | | ❌ | ✅ | 365 only – assign names to variables inside formulas | | | ❌ | ✅ | 365 only – create custom functions | If you use an Office 365 account provided by your school, you have all of these. If you bought a perpetual‑license version like Office 2021, support for new functions is limited. Extended 2: Function Example (Office 365) – returns all rows from columns A through C where column B equals “Sales”. No manual filtering or copying needed. Extended 3: Excel Tables Select your data and press to convert a normal range into an Excel Table. Benefits: When you add new data, formulas and formatting automatically extend Column headers automatically have filter buttons Formulas use structured references like , which are much more readable than Part 3: PowerPoint I would like someone more experienced than me to write this part. For now, it is left intentionally blank. Extended: VBA Macros VBA (Visual Basic for Applications) is the programming language built into Office. You can write scripts to automate repetitive tasks. Open the VBA editor: What VBA Can Do Batch processing Word documents: Change the margins of every Word document in a folder to 2.5 cm. Doing this manually means opening each document and clicking many times. With a short VBA script, you can process hundreds of documents with one click. Excel automation: Combine 12 monthly data sheets into one master sheet. Write a loop that automatically opens each file, copies the data, and pastes it into a summary sheet. PowerPoint batch operations: Add a company logo to the top‑right corner of every slide in a 200‑slide deck. Recording Macros The easiest method: Go to the “Developer” tab → “Record Macro” → perform your actions (e.g., set margins, change fonts) → “Stop Recording”. Excel automatically translates your actions into VBA code. You can then replay that macro with a single click. Note: Recorded macros generate code that is verbose (it records every single step, including some you might not need). But it is a great way to learn – record an action, look at the generated code, then start tweaking it. Security , , and are macro‑enabled files. When you open such a file, Office warns you that “the file contains macros”. Only open macro‑enabled files from trusted sources (e.g., your school, a colleague). Never open them from unknown origins – macros can delete files, format your hard drive, or do other harmful things. Macros are essentially small executable programs. Viewing and editing macros: Press to open the VBA editor, where you can see all modules and code. You do not need to be a programmer to gain something – being able to recognise basic logic words like “Open”, “Copy”, “Paste” is already useful.

title: LaTeX
content: Appendix 11: LaTeX This appendix introduces the basics of LaTeX. LaTeX is a typesetting system designed for academic papers, especially good for mathematical formulas and references. If you plan to publish papers or write a thesis, you will likely encounter it. This appendix uses Shanghai Jiao Tong University's thesis template (SJTUThesis) as an example to show how to write LaTeX documents with VS Code. Please note: The content below is for reference only. Always follow the specific formatting requirements given by your university instructors or journal guidelines. The goal is simply to help you get familiar with LaTeX. 11.1 What Is LaTeX? LaTeX (pronounced "lah-tekh" or "lay-tekh") is different from Word. Word is "what you see is what you get" – you type, and it immediately shows the formatted result. LaTeX is "what you think is what you get" – you write code (a markup language), then compile it to produce a PDF. Advantages: Formatting is automatically consistent – no accidental mixing of fonts or sizes Mathematical formulas look beautiful References are automatically numbered and sorted Long documents (dozens or hundreds of pages) rarely become sluggish Disadvantages: There is a learning curve; you will need to look things up when errors occur You must compile to see the result, unlike Word's live update Many science and engineering departments require theses and journal papers to be typeset in LaTeX. Your university may provide a template (e.g., the document class), and you simply fill in your content. 11.2 Setting Up the Environment: TeX Distribution + VS Code To write LaTeX, you first need a "compilation environment" – a TeX distribution. The most common one is TeX Live (works on Windows, Linux, and macOS). 11.2.1 Installing TeX Live Download the TeX Live ISO file from Tsinghua University's TUNA mirror. Extract or mount the ISO, then run (Windows) or (Linux/macOS). Choose "full installation" (scheme-full) to avoid missing packages later. The installation may take about half an hour. After installation, open a command line and type . If you see version information, the installation succeeded. Additional note: About latexmk and Perl (Windows users) The compilation tool is a Perl script. TeX Live comes with its own Perl interpreter ( ), so normally works right after installation. If you get a "command not found" error when typing , it means TeX Live's directory is not in your system PATH. You can re‑run the installer and check "Add to PATH", or add it manually (see Appendix 9 for environment variables). 11.2.2 Installing VS Code and the LaTeX Workshop Extension If you have not already installed VS Code, do so first (see Appendix 7). Once installed, go to the Extensions Marketplace, search for LaTeX Workshop, and install it. This extension provides syntax highlighting, automatic compilation, forward/backward search, and more. 11.2.3 Configuring VS Code (Optional but Recommended) Open VS Code settings ( ), search for , and change the default compilation recipe to . This will automatically compile whenever you save a file. Alternatively, place a file in your project folder: 11.3 A Real Template: SJTUThesis Shanghai Jiao Tong University's thesis template, SJTUThesis, is a complete LaTeX project. You can find it on GitHub ( ). Download and unzip it, then open the folder in VS Code. You will see several files and folders. 11.3.1 First Step After Downloading: Try to Compile The three most common problems on the first compilation Problem 1: Missing fonts Many university templates require SimSun, SimHei, and Times New Roman fonts. Windows comes with these fonts, so no issue there. macOS users may need to install SimSun manually (copy it from a Windows machine, or use a command like ). Linux users – I trust you can figure it out. Problem 2: Missing packages If the compilation error says , you are missing a package. Install it using TeX Live's : If is not found, run it as administrator (Windows) or with (Linux/macOS). You may need to switch to a different mirror – see the TUNA mirror documentation. Problem 3: Encoding errors An error like usually means the file is not saved as UTF-8. In VS Code, click the encoding indicator at the bottom‑right, then choose “Save with Encoding” → UTF-8. 11.3.2 Main File Structure | File/folder | Purpose | |-------------|---------| | | The master file – the "skeleton" of your thesis. It includes chapters via | | | Configuration: your name, thesis title, department, etc. | | | Reference database (BibTeX format) | | | Holds the chapter files, e.g., , | | | Holds image files | | | The template's style file (generally you do not need to modify it) | 11.3.3 The Skeleton of When writing your thesis, you will only need to edit the chapter files under and the personal information in . The master file usually does not need to be touched. 11.4 How to Write Content 11.4.1 Chapters and Headings Inside a chapter file (e.g., ): Write your text directly. A blank line indicates a paragraph break. 11.4.2 Mathematical Formulas (Basics) Inline formulas are wrapped in : Displayed equations (with numbering) use the environment: Common symbols inside formulas: Superscripts and subscripts: , Fractions: Square roots: , Summation: Integration: Greek letters: , , , , , etc. 11.4.3 Mathematical Formulas (Intermediate) Multi‑line equations (align environment) When an equation is too long to fit on one line, or you need to align at equal signs, use the environment: marks the alignment point (usually placed before the equal sign), and ends a line. To suppress numbering on a particular line, add before : Matrices Use (parentheses), (square brackets), (vertical bars), etc.: Ellipses: (horizontal), (vertical), (diagonal): Piecewise functions (cases environment) 11.4.4 Figures Place your image files in the folder (PDF, PNG, or JPG are recommended). Then insert a figure in a chapter file: tells LaTeX that the figure can be placed here, at the top of a page, at the bottom, or on a separate float page. LaTeX automatically chooses the best position. centres the figure. sets the figure width to 80% of the text width. sets the caption; the figure number (e.g., “Figure 3.1”) is generated automatically. defines a label so you can reference it in the text: . Note: Do not use spaces or Chinese characters in image file names or paths, otherwise LaTeX may not find them. Use English names like . Subfigures (side‑by‑side figures) When you need to place two or more images side‑by‑side with separate (a), (b) captions, use the package: Make sure to load the package at the beginning of the document: . University templates usually already include it. 11.4.5 Tables Writing tables in LaTeX can be somewhat tedious. A practical approach is to use an online tool (like Tables Generator) to generate the code and then paste it. Here is a simple three‑line table example: The package provides , , and . The template should already load it. Long tables that span multiple pages (longtable) If you have a very long table (e.g., several pages of experimental data), a normal + cannot break across pages – the table will be cut off at the page boundary. In this case, use the package: differs from ordinary tables in that it can break across pages, and the header is repeated at the top of each page. The downside is less flexible float placement, but for long tables it is the only practical option. 11.4.6 References (Basics) References are stored in a file in BibTeX format. A sample entry (from ): In the body of your thesis, cite it: After compilation, the reference list is automatically generated where appears. Citation numbers and the list formatting follow the required standard (e.g., GB/T 7714 for Chinese theses). Important notes on the field: Separate multiple authors with (not commas): LaTeX uses to distinguish authors, automatically producing “Li, X. D., Zhang, Q. H., & Ye, J. L.” or “Li et al.” as needed Do not write – the whole string would be treated as a single author 11.4.7 References (Intermediate) Where to get BibTeX entries for Chinese publications CNKI (China National Knowledge Infrastructure): On the article detail page, look for “Export” → “BibTeX” → copy the content. However, CNKI‑exported BibTeX often has problems (e.g., missing between authors, incorrect format). After exporting, manually check and fix: Check : if it shows , change it to Check : it should be , not Check journal name: CNKI sometimes puts the journal name in instead of – move it if needed Google Scholar: Below the search result, click “Cite” → “BibTeX” and copy directly. The quality is generally better than CNKI. Recommended workflow: Use Zotero (free reference manager). With the browser plugin, you can capture references with one click. Zotero automatically recognises the fields, and you can export a file. Zotero also integrates with Word/LaTeX, greatly reducing manual entry errors. Why references might not show up If after compilation you see in the text, or the reference list is empty, the compilation order is likely wrong. The correct sequence is: → generates auxiliary files → processes the file → writes references into the document → resolves cross‑references (optional but recommended) With VS Code’s LaTeX Workshop using the recipe, this order is handled automatically. If you use the command line, run: automatically detects how many passes are needed and whether is required. 11.4.8 Three Common Pitfalls for Beginners Pitfall 1: Blank lines causing paragraph indentation In LaTeX, a blank line means a paragraph break. If you have two consecutive lines of text separated by a blank line, the second paragraph will have an indented first line (as is customary in Chinese typography). Many people do not want this indentation and manually add – but doing that for every paragraph is tedious. The correct approach: For Chinese theses, first‑line indentation is usually required, so you do not need to change anything. If you really need a paragraph without indentation (e.g., for a figure caption), write just before that paragraph. If you want to disable indentation globally, add in the preamble, but this will deviate from most university formatting requirements – not recommended. Pitfall 2: Abusing to force line breaks Using inside a regular paragraph forces a line break but does not create a new paragraph. The next line will not have indentation, and line breaks may appear in odd places. Wrong: Right: Let LaTeX wrap lines automatically. If you genuinely need a line break without a new paragraph, use . If you want a new paragraph, use a blank line. Pitfall 3: Figures not showing Missing figures usually have three causes: Wrong path: but the folder is named (missing the ‘s’) – case sensitivity also matters Spaces or Chinese characters in the file name: → rename to Unsupported format: When compiling with , supported formats are PNG, JPG, and PDF. If you use , PDF is the most reliable. As a rule, use PDF (especially for vector graphics) Debugging tip: Look at the compilation log (in VS Code, LaTeX Workshop’s “LaTeX Compiler” output window) and search for . 11.5 How to Compile 11.5.1 Compiling in VS Code Press (or click “Build LaTeX project” in the left sidebar) – this triggers automatic compilation. After a successful build, is generated. LaTeX Workshop uses the recipe by default, which handles multiple passes and references automatically. If compilation fails: Open VS Code’s “Output” panel ( ), then choose “LaTeX Compiler” from the dropdown menu Look for error messages in red, and search online for the error text See the Extended Reading section for common error messages and solutions 11.5.2 Compiling from the Command Line If you prefer the command line, navigate to the project folder (where is) and run: If you get a “command not found” error for , the Perl environment is not set up correctly. Refer back to the extra note in section 11.2.1. If you prefer not to use , you can manually run the steps: Note: The command handles references. Some older templates use instead (command: ). The modern version of SJTUThesis uses . 11.5.3 Using the Template’s Built‑in Compilation Script Many LaTeX templates provide a (Linux/macOS) or (Windows). For SJTUThesis: Windows: double‑click , or run it from the command line Linux/macOS: run in the terminal (requires to be installed) 11.6 A Minimal Example Below is a “minimal paper fragment” that does not rely on any complex template. Copy it into a file and try compiling it. Compiling this produces a PDF document with formulas, section headings, automatic numbering, etc. Extended Reading The following content covers more advanced LaTeX topics. Refer to it when you outgrow the basics. Extended 1: What Are Packages (Macros)? LaTeX’s functionality is extended through “packages”. When you write at the beginning of your document, you are loading a package for mathematical formulas. Commonly used packages: : inserting images , : advanced mathematical features : setting page margins : generating hyperlinks and bookmarks : three‑line tables : multi‑page tables : subfigures (side‑by‑side figures) : algorithm environments Extended 2: Reference Management Tools If you have many references, consider using dedicated reference management software such as Zotero (free) or JabRef. They allow you to import reference entries from journal websites with a single click and then export a file. Zotero also has a plugin (Better BibTeX) that generates stable citekeys and can integrate directly with VS Code or Overleaf. Extended 3: Common Compilation Errors and Solutions | Error message | Likely cause | Solution | |---------------|--------------|----------| | | An undefined command was used | Check spelling, or load the required package | | | Missing package | | | | Encoding issue | Save the file as UTF‑8 | | | Forgot to load the package | Add , or change to | | | Didn't run | Run then recompile | | appears in the text | Incorrect citation label | Check that the key in matches the key in the file | | Figure not shown; only the file name appears | Unsupported format or wrong path | Check the file name (no spaces or Chinese characters); try PDF format | Extended 4: Forward and Inverse Search Forward search: In the file, hold and click on a line – you jump to the corresponding location in the PDF. Inverse search: Double‑click a line in the PDF – you jump back to the corresponding line in the file. LaTeX Workshop supports forward search by default. Inverse search on Windows may require extra configuration (setting SumatraPDF as the default PDF viewer). For beginners, this is not essential. Extended 5: Template Document Class ( ) and Configuration ( ) The style of the SJTU template is written in . Ordinary users do not need to modify it. Only if you are creating a document class from scratch would you need to write a file. For a thesis, using the template provided by your university is the safest approach. Extended 6: Overleaf – Online LaTeX Editor If you do not want to install TeX Live locally, you can use an online LaTeX editor – for example, Overleaf ( ), or Chinese alternatives like TeXPage or SJTU LaTeX Document Assistant. You simply register an account, upload a template (or choose one from the template library), and write LaTeX in your browser with real‑time preview. This is an excellent way for beginners to get started quickly. Comparison between Overleaf and a local environment: | Feature | Overleaf | Local (TeX Live + VS Code) | |---------|----------|----------------------------| | Installation cost | Zero – register and use | Download 4–5 GB, ~30 minutes to install | | Compilation speed | Depends on server load | Depends on your computer (generally faster) | | Offline use | No | Yes | | Chinese template support | Need to upload fonts | Fonts managed by the OS | | Collaborative editing | Native support | Needs Git or other tools | For beginners, it is recommended to start with Overleaf to get your first document working, then decide whether to install a local environment.

title: OpenSource
content: Appendix 12: Open Source This appendix introduces the basic concepts of open source software, common open source licenses, and a few noteworthy open source projects. This material is not essential for everyday computer use, but it is good to understand – much of the computers, phones, and internet you use today are built on open source software. 12.1 What Is Open Source Open source means that a piece of software's source code is open to everyone. Anyone can view, modify, and distribute that code. The opposite of open source is proprietary software – the source code is not public. Users can only run the compiled program; they cannot see how it works or modify it. Windows, Microsoft Office, Photoshop, and Steam are all proprietary software. Open source does not mean free of charge. Many open source programs are indeed free to use, but the core meaning of "open source" is about freedom – freedom to use, to study, to modify, and to share. Some open source products are sold (e.g., enterprise editions or paid support). 12.2 Free Software vs. Open Source Software These two terms are often used interchangeably, but their underlying philosophies differ slightly. Free Software is a concept promoted by the Free Software Foundation (FSF) , founded by Richard Stallman in 1985. Here "free" refers to freedom of speech, not free beer. The FSF emphasises the ethical dimension: users should have control over the software, not the other way around. Open Source Software emerged a bit later (1998) and focuses more on technical advantages: opening the source code leads to better quality, higher security, and faster iteration. The term deliberately avoids the ideological language of "free software", making it more palatable to businesses and the commercial world. In practice, the two overlap heavily – most free software is also open source, and vice versa. But in spirit, the FSF is more "hardcore", emphasising user rights and ethics, while the open source movement is more pragmatic, focusing on collaboration and efficiency. 12.3 Open Source Licenses An open source license specifies what others can do with your code and what conditions they must follow. Different licenses vary significantly, and choosing the wrong one can create legal risks. 12.3.1 Permissive Licenses These licenses place few restrictions on users. You can take the code, use it, modify it, and even release your modified version as closed source (without sharing your changes), as long as you retain the original copyright notice. MIT License: One of the simplest licenses. It says only two things: keep the copyright notice, and don't hold the author liable. Many small Node.js and Python projects use it. Apache License 2.0: Similar to MIT, but adds a few clauses: it explicitly grants patent rights (to avoid certain patent traps) and requires you to state which files you modified. Projects from the Apache Software Foundation – such as Hadoop and Kubernetes – use this license. BSD License: Very similar to MIT. There are several variants (2‑Clause, 3‑Clause, 4‑Clause). The differences involve whether you can use the author's name for advertising and whether all derivative works must retain the original author's information. FreeBSD and early versions of the Go language use BSD licenses. 12.3.2 Strong (Copyleft) Licenses These licenses require that your modifications and derivative works must also be open sourced under the same license. GPL (GNU General Public License) : The most famous copyleft license. If a piece of software uses GPL‑licensed code, then the entire software must be released under the GPL. The Linux kernel, Git, and the GCC compiler all use the GPL. GPLv2: The version used by the Linux kernel. GPLv3: Released in 2007, adding provisions about patents and anti‑circumvention. Some projects (including the Linux kernel) consider v3 too strict and stick with v2. LGPL (Lesser GPL) : A relaxed version of the GPL. If you only link to an LGPL library (e.g., use a or ), your own code does not need to be open source. However, if you modify the library itself, those modifications must be open sourced. Often used for function libraries such as GTK and parts of FFmpeg. AGPL (Affero GPL) : The GPL has a loophole: if you run GPL code on a server and users only interact with it over the network (without receiving a copy of the software), you are not required to release your code. AGPL closes this loophole – providing a service over the network counts as distribution, so you must open source your code. Early versions of MongoDB used the AGPL. 12.3.3 Which One Should You Choose? | Your goal | Recommended license | |-----------|---------------------| | Let anyone use the code, even in closed‑source commercial products | MIT / Apache 2.0 | | Ensure the code and all derivatives remain forever open source | GPL | | You are writing a library – allow others to link to it without forcing their code open | LGPL | | You offer a network service and don't want someone to take it, tweak the UI, and sell it closed‑source | AGPL | Choosing a "wrong" license is not a disaster – you can change it later. However, if you use GPL‑licensed code in your project, your code must be released under the GPL. This is a legal requirement, not a suggestion. 12.4 Mirror Sites A mirror site is a replica of a large software repository or open source project. Because the original servers are often outside China, access can be slow and unreliable. Universities and companies inside China set up mirrors that synchronise regularly with the original sources, allowing domestic users to download at high speed. Some of the best‑known mirrors in China: Tsinghua University TUNA Mirror: Large, fast‑updating, and comprehensive. Many of the software download links recommended earlier in this guide come from here. USTC (University of Science and Technology of China) UTSC Mirror: Similarly long‑standing and broad in coverage. Shanghai Jiao Tong University SJTUG Mirror: One of the download locations for the SJTUThesis template. Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, Huawei Cloud : They also run open source mirrors, focusing on operating systems and development tools. How to use: Different package managers have different methods for changing the mirror source. I recommend searching on your own. Example search query: 12.5 Notable Open Source Software You may not have used the following open source applications, but they run quietly behind the scenes in many industries. It's enough to know their names and what they do. 12.5.1 The Linux Kernel Linux is an open source operating system kernel, released by Linus Torvalds in 1991. It is not a complete operating system like Windows, but the lowest‑level core of the system – managing hardware, processes, memory, and the file system. Android – the OS on your phone – runs on the Linux kernel. More than 70% of the world's servers run Linux. Routers, smart TVs, car infotainment systems, ATMs, supercomputers – the vast majority run Linux. Without Linux, the internet as we know it would not exist. 12.5.2 GIMP GIMP (GNU Image Manipulation Program) : An open source image editing application, often described as the "open source alternative to Photoshop". It is very powerful – layers, filters, masks, paths, colour adjustments – all present. The interface is different from Photoshop and requires some learning. Suitable for people who do not want to pay for Photoshop but need to edit images occasionally. 12.5.3 LibreOffice LibreOffice: An open source office suite, comprising Writer (documents), Calc (spreadsheets), Impress (presentations), Draw (drawing), and Base (databases). It is compatible with Microsoft Office formats ( , , all open). The interface is a bit rougher than Office, but it is the standard default on Linux systems. If you do not want to subscribe to Office 365, give it a try. 12.5.4 Krita Krita: An open source digital painting application, aimed at illustrators and concept artists. Its brush engine is very powerful, supporting pressure sensitivity, stabilisation, and brush smoothing. The comic features (storyboarding, speech bubbles) are also mature. The difference from GIMP: GIMP is more like Photoshop (general image editing), while Krita is more like Procreate / Painter (dedicated drawing). Many animation studios use it. 12.5.5 Blender Blender: An open source 3D creation suite. Modelling, sculpting, materials, rendering, animation, video editing, compositing – it does everything. Once dismissed as "amateur software", it is now an industrial‑grade tool that can compete with Maya and 3ds Max. The Hollywood animated film Spider‑Man: Into the Spider‑Verse used Blender, and some promotional videos for Arknights and Genshin Impact were made with Blender. The learning curve is steep, but it is completely free. 12.5.6 VLC VLC: An open source multimedia player. Similar to PotPlayer, but VLC is cross‑platform (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS). It can play almost any video format without requiring extra codecs. Small footprint, fast startup, and can also act as a network streaming client. We recommended PotPlayer earlier; VLC is a good alternative. 12.5.7 7‑Zip / NanaZip 7‑Zip: An open source compression tool. NanaZip, recommended earlier, is a modernised interface for 7‑Zip. The core 7z format achieves higher compression ratios than ZIP. Its command‑line version is used in many automation scripts. 12.5.8 FFmpeg FFmpeg: An open source command‑line tool for audio and video processing. It is the Swiss Army knife for video professionals. You can use it to convert formats, cut clips, merge videos, extract audio, burn subtitles. OBS, VLC, YouTube, and Netflix all use FFmpeg behind the scenes. It was mentioned earlier in the video processing section. 12.5.9 OBS Studio OBS (Open Broadcaster Software) : An open source tool for live streaming and screen recording. Compared to the paid XSplit, OBS is no less capable and is completely free. It supports multiple scenes, multiple sources, filters, and streaming. Many game streamers and online course recorders use it. Its configuration was covered in Chapter 4. 12.5.10 VS Code VS Code: Microsoft's open source code editor. Recommended in Appendix 7 – with plugins, it can do almost anything. Although developed by Microsoft, the code is open source (MIT license). Some joke that "Microsoft is now one of the largest open source contributors" – Azure documentation, TypeScript, .NET Core are all open sourced. 12.5.11 osu! osu!: An open source music rhythm game. Players click, drag, and spin along with the music. There are four modes (standard, taiko, catch the fruit, piano). The community is very active, with millions of user‑made beatmaps. It has excellent tablet support – many people play it with a drawing tablet. The game itself is free and open source, sustained by donations and paid skins. 12.6 A Final Thought The computer you use today – opening a browser (Chromium engine), watching videos (FFmpeg decoding), chatting (Linux servers forwarding messages), browsing forums (hosted by Nginx or Apache) – all of it runs on open source projects. You may never need to read a single line of kernel code, nor submit a pull request to any project. But knowing that these things exist, knowing where they came from and under what rules they operate, will deepen your understanding of the digital world. They are not perfect, but without them, today's world would not look the same. 12.7 Creative Commons Licenses (CC) Creative Commons (CC) is not a software open source license. It is a set of public licenses for creative works – articles, images, music, videos, blog posts, courseware, Wikipedia entries, and more. The goal is to allow creators to proactively declare "how others may use my work", instead of defaulting to "all rights reserved". 12.7.1 Why CC Licenses Exist Traditional copyright defaults to "All Rights Reserved". You draw a picture and upload it. If someone wants to share it, translate it, or turn it into a wallpaper, legally they must ask your permission first. In practice this is very inefficient: many authors are unreachable, or they would not mind sharing but have never explicitly said so. CC licenses provide a standardised set of "Some Rights Reserved" statements. A creator can clearly tell everyone: you may copy, share, modify, and even commercially use my work, as long as you meet my conditions (e.g., attribution, non‑commercial use). 12.7.2 The Four Core Elements All CC licenses are built from combinations of the following four conditions: | Icon | Abbr | Condition | Meaning | |------|------|-----------|---------| | | BY | Attribution | You must credit the author, the work's title, and the license. All CC licenses include BY. | | | SA | ShareAlike | Modified works must be released under the same license. Similar to GPL's copyleft. | | | NC | NonCommercial | Only non‑commercial uses are allowed. Commercial use requires separate permission. | | | ND | NoDerivatives | You may copy and share, but not modify, adapt, or create derivatives. | 12.7.3 The Six Main CC Licenses Combining the above conditions gives six common licenses, from most permissive to most restrictive: | Abbreviation | Full name | Conditions | What is allowed | |--------------|-----------|------------|------------------| | CC BY | Attribution | BY | Any use (including commercial), can modify, can release derivatives under a different license. | | CC BY-SA | Attribution-ShareAlike | BY + SA | Any use, can modify, but derivatives must use the same license. Wikipedia uses this. | | CC BY-NC | Attribution-NonCommercial | BY + NC | Can share and modify, but non‑commercial only; can change the license. | | CC BY-NC-SA | Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike | BY + NC + SA | Non‑commercial only, can modify, but derivatives must use the same license. | | CC BY-ND | Attribution-NoDerivatives | BY + ND | Can share (including commercially), but cannot modify. | | CC BY-NC-ND | Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives | BY + NC + ND | Most restrictive. Can only share as‑is, no modifications, no commercial use. | 12.7.4 CC0 and the Public Domain There is also a special version: CC0 (Public Domain Dedication) . A creator who chooses CC0 dedicates their work to the public domain – they waive all copyright rights. Anyone can use, modify, or commercially exploit the work without attribution and without any conditions. CC0 is not one of the "six licenses". It is a separate "no copyright" declaration. Some images on Unsplash, OpenStreetMap data, and certain academic databases use CC0. The public domain refers to works whose copyright has expired (e.g., the author died more than 70 years ago – varies by jurisdiction) or has been voluntarily waived. All CC licenses (including CC0) are logically "copyright‑based open permissions", whereas the public domain is "no copyright" – legally even more absolute. 12.7.5 License Versions CC licenses have gone through several versions: 1.0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, and 4.0. 4.0 is the latest (released 2013) . It fixes many legal issues, is more international, and is easier to interoperate with other licenses. When choosing a license, prefer version 4.0. Some older works may be marked 3.0 or 2.5 – those are still legally valid, but their porting to different jurisdictions may vary. 12.7.6 Typical Choices for Different Scenarios | Your goal | Recommended license | |-----------|---------------------| | You wrote a popular science article and want it widely read – you don't mind others adapting it into videos or even selling it, as long as you are credited | CC BY | | You drew an illustration – others may use it as wallpaper or print it on T‑shirts, but cannot sell those items | CC BY-NC | | You wrote a technical tutorial – others may translate, modify, and republish it, but the translated version must also be open (similar to GPL) | CC BY-SA | | You took a photo – others may use it freely, but they cannot crop out your watermark or alter it beyond recognition | CC BY-ND | | Your thesis is uploaded to the university repository – you want it to be downloadable and shared, but not modified or sold | CC BY-NC-ND | | You took a casual snapshot and truly don't care if someone uses it on a commercial poster | CC0 | 12.7.7 How to Find CC‑Licensed Works Images: Flickr's "Advanced Search" lets you filter by CC license. Unsplash images are mostly CC0 or similar terms. Wikimedia Commons files all have clear CC labels. Music: Free Music Archive (FMA), Jamendo. The YouTube Audio Library also has a CC category. Text: Wikipedia (CC BY‑SA). Some articles on Medium (look at the footer). Courseware: MIT OpenCourseWare (CC BY‑NC‑SA). Some resources from Chinese university MOOCs. 12.7.8 A Friendly Reminder CC licenses are legal tools based on copyright. They are effective in China as well (Chinese copyright law recognises the granting of partial rights through licenses). However, keep in mind: Works marked NC (NonCommercial) cannot be sold. What counts as "commercial"? Using them in internal company training, printing them on products for sale, putting them behind a paywall – all of these are commercial uses. Works marked ND (NoDerivatives) cannot be translated, remixed, or adapted. Simple copying and sharing is fine. If you fail to meet a condition (e.g., forget to provide attribution), your permission to use the work automatically ends – unless you obtain separate permission from the author. In addition to the human‑readable deed (a summary) and the machine‑readable metadata, every CC license has a full legal code. In case of disputes, the legal code governs.

title: LaptopBasics
content: Appendix 1: Laptop Basics This chapter covers only the most essential concepts and operations. If you have never used a computer before, start here. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section at the end. 1.1 Hardware Basics 1.1.1 What is a CPU The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the computing and control core of a computer. It interprets instructions, processes data, and coordinates all components. Think of it as the "brain" of the machine. 1.1.2 What is a GPU The GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) specializes in graphics and parallel computing. Laptop GPUs come in two forms: Integrated GPU (iGPU): packaged inside the same chip as the CPU, has no dedicated video memory – it borrows a portion of system RAM. Discrete GPU (dGPU): a separate chip with its own video memory. 1.1.3 What is RAM (Memory) RAM is the temporary warehouse where the CPU reads and writes data directly. It is fast, but loses all data when power is cut. When you open a program, the system copies its data from the storage drive to RAM. 1.1.4 What is a Storage Drive The storage drive holds data permanently – data survives after shutdown. Modern laptops almost exclusively use Solid‑State Drives (SSDs). 1.1.5 The Difference Between RAM and Storage Use a kitchen counter and a fridge as a metaphor: RAM is the countertop: the ingredients you are actively chopping and preparing are right in front of you for quick access. Counter space is limited, and when you finish cooking (power is cut), any leftover ingredients on the counter are thrown away. Storage is the refrigerator: all ingredients are kept there for the long term, and you take them out to the counter when needed. 1.2 Integrated vs. Discrete GPU (Basic Concepts) iGPU: low power, low heat – suitable for office work, web browsing, and light gaming. dGPU: high performance – suitable for demanding games, 3D modelling, video editing, etc. Real‑world gaming performance of iGPUs is limited by thermal and power constraints; see Extended Reading. 1.3 Touchpads (What You Need to Know) High‑end thin‑and‑light laptops in 2026 use mostly two types of touchpads: Haptic touchpad: cannot be pressed when the device is off. When powered, it detects pressure via sensors and provides vibration feedback through a haptic motor. The feel depends entirely on the manufacturer's tuning. Full‑area mechanical touchpad: the entire surface clicks down (unlike traditional touchpads where only the bottom half moves). However, on many Windows laptops, the required force differs between the top and bottom areas. Strongly recommended: go to an Apple store and try the MacBook Pro's haptic touchpad (the industry benchmark for haptic feedback) and the MacBook Neo's full‑area mechanical touchpad (the benchmark for that type). Get a feel for their uniform, responsive clicks. Then come back and try Windows counterparts – you will immediately know what level of quality you can accept. 1.4 Laptop Classifications Thin and light: portable, long battery life, quiet. Uses low‑power CPU, no discrete GPU. Thickness around 15mm, weight under 1.3kg. Suitable for office work, study, light entertainment. Gaming laptop: high performance, with a high‑power CPU and mid‑range to high‑end discrete GPU. Heavy cooling, weight often exceeds 2kg. Suitable for demanding games, professional video editing, etc. All‑rounder / creator laptop: sits between the two – somewhat portable (around 1.8kg), with an entry‑level or mid‑range discrete GPU. Can handle office work and light gaming. 1.5 Buying Reference: 笔吧评测室 笔吧评测室 is one of the more authoritative laptop review sources in China. Follow their WeChat public account or Bilibili channel (also on Douyin and Xiaohongshu). Their WeChat account publishes weekly curated recommendations by price range, with detailed explanations. Read those to narrow down a few candidate models, then search for in‑depth reviews and user feedback. 1.6 Purchase Advice (2026) Prices are high: laptop prices are at historical highs in 2026. If you are not in urgent need (e.g., your current computer still works), you can wait – prices will likely drop. If you must buy: thin‑and‑light laptops offer better value in the current market. The iGPU performance of modern high‑end thin‑and‑light laptops is sufficient for many games and daily software. Government subsidies: many provinces offer 10‑20% consumer subsidies. If possible, consider travelling to a province with such subsidies to buy your laptop. Search for "province name + appliance subsidy" for details. 1.7 From Unboxing to Activation: Inspection Procedure (Core Steps) When you receive your laptop, follow these steps. Before activation, you have unconditional return rights. If you find any problem, return it immediately – do not attempt to fix it yourself. Check the packaging and exterior Confirm that the seals are intact. Inspect the lid (A‑cover) and bottom (D‑cover) for scratches or dents. Check the power adapter and charging port for signs of use. Gently open and close the lid a few times; listen for creaking. For a mechanical (traditional hinged) touchpad: gently wiggle the edges to see if it rocks, and press all four corners to feel for consistent resistance. For a haptic touchpad: test the feedback in different areas after booting into the OS. Lightly press different areas of the keyboard to feel for overall rigidity. If you find any anomaly that you couldn't accept, take photos at once and contact customer service for a return. Transport mode test Do not plug in the power adapter. Press the power button once. If it does not turn on → normal, proceed. If it turns on and boots into the OS immediately → the unit has been used. Return it immediately. First boot setup (skip internet) When you reach the login screen, do not connect to Wi‑Fi. To bypass Windows 11's forced internet requirement: At the region selection screen, press to open Command Prompt. Type and press Enter. The system will restart. After reboot, when you reach the "Let's connect you to a network" screen, click "I don't have internet" → "Continue with limited setup". Log in with a local account (use an English alphanumeric username). Screen inspection After entering the desktop, right‑click → Personalize → Background → Choose a solid color. Cycle through pure white, pure black, pure red, pure green, and pure blue. Carefully look for dead pixels (unexpected bright or dark dots). On a pure black background, check for backlight bleed. Minor IPS glow at the edges is normal, but if a corner glows like a small flashlight, consider a return. Verify the configuration Press Win + X → Task Manager → Performance to confirm CPU model and RAM capacity. Download a drive inspection tool (e.g., CrystalDiskInfo) to check the SSD's brand and model against reviews. CrystalDiskInfo's Offical Download Site: Or you may download with Usability test Lift the laptop with one hand – any unusual creaking? Plug in a USB drive and a mouse; confirm all ports work. After fully charging, use it on battery for an hour of light use to rule out abnormal battery drain. 7‑day no‑questions‑asked return If you find any of the following: dead pixels (especially in the centre), backlight bleed affecting normal viewing, abnormal touchpad click feel, unusual battery wear, or widespread reports of a defect in this batch – directly request a return (not an exchange) and either reorder or switch to another brand. Create a Microsoft account and activate Go to signup.live.com and create a free account. Log in to activate the pre‑installed Office suite (within 30 days, otherwise the license may expire). With an account, you can digitally reactivate Windows after a clean reinstall without entering a product key. Finally, connect to the internet After all checks are complete, connect to Wi‑Fi. Windows and Office will activate automatically. Extended Reading The following sections contain detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the must‑read part. Extended 1: CPU Models and Performance Mainstream thin‑and‑light laptops in 2026 use CPUs such as the Intel Core Ultra 5 338H、Ultra X7 358H、Ultra X9 388H. Mainstream gaming laptops often pair an Intel Ultra 7 356H with an NVIDIA RTX 5060 or 5070. Laptop CPU naming can be confusing – the same architecture may spawn multiple model numbers. For example, AMD's 8845H is essentially a rebranded 7845H (identical specifications, only the name differs). Always search for performance reviews of the exact model before buying; do not judge by the numbers alone. Extended 2: iGPU Gaming – Expectations vs. Reality Some marketing claims "iGPU performance close to an RTX 3050 Ti". However, note that an iGPU has no dedicated video memory – it borrows system RAM – and the CPU and iGPU share the same thermal solution. Under sustained gaming loads, the CPU and iGPU compete for power and thermal headroom, so real‑world performance often falls short of benchmark numbers. If you plan to play AAA games on an iGPU laptop, watch game‑specific tests by reviewers like 笔吧评测室 before deciding. Extended 3: Sleep States (S0ix vs. S3) Windows defines several power sleep states. S3, known as "Suspend to RAM", powers down the CPU and most hardware while keeping RAM refreshed – wake‑up is very fast (about 1‑2 seconds). S0ix (Modern Standby, also called S2idle) is a low‑power idle state promoted by Microsoft since Windows 8, allowing the system to stay connected and update while the screen is off – similar to a smartphone. However, it can cause heat, battery drain, and unreliable wake‑up. Since Intel Meteor Lake (12th‑gen Core), Microsoft has required hardware vendors to drop full support for S3. Consequently, many new laptops support only S0ix. Even running Linux, the ACPI tables are stripped of S3 code, making reliable sleep impossible. If sleep reliability matters to you, check community feedback before buying – some business laptops (e.g., certain ThinkPad models) still retain S3 options. Extended 4: Touchpad Tuning Differences Even among haptic touchpads, the vibration feedback varies greatly by manufacturer – for example, Xiaomi and Honor feel completely different. Therefore, it is worth visiting a physical store to try them yourself. If you are unsure what you like, first try the MacBook Pro's haptic touchpad (the industry benchmark) and the MacBook Neo's full‑area mechanical touchpad (also a benchmark). Then compare with Windows laptops – you will clearly see what level of quality you can accept. Extended 5: Storage Drive Selection NAND Manufacturers vs. Assembly Houses The core of an SSD is the NAND flash chip. Companies that manufacture their own NAND are called NAND manufacturers or IDMs. Major active NAND manufacturers include Samsung, SK hynix (including the acquired Intel NAND business, now Solidigm), Micron, Kioxia, Western Digital, and China's YMTC. YMTC's Xtacking architecture (e.g., X4‑9040) is competitive in both performance and cost. The controller is the "small CPU" of an SSD, handling data management, wear leveling, garbage collection, etc. Notable retail controller vendors include Silicon Motion, Phison, Maxio, and InnoGrit. TLC vs. QLC TLC (Triple‑Level Cell): stores 3 bits per cell – good write endurance and speed. QLC (Quad‑Level Cell): stores 4 bits per cell – higher density, lower cost, but significantly worse write endurance and write speed. For a system drive or frequent large writes, QLC is generally not recommended. The Solidigm P41 Plus is a rare exception – its excellent firmware mitigates QLC's drawbacks. Original vs. Third‑party SSDs Original SSD: designed, packaged, and sold by the NAND manufacturer itself – e.g., Samsung, Western Digital, Kioxia, ZhiTai. Third‑party SSD: buys raw NAND wafers and then packages, tests, and assembles them – e.g., Kingston, ADATA. Quality depends on the vendor's packaging capability. Vendors with their own packaging and rigorous testing (e.g., UMIS's UnionMemory brand) are acceptable. Avoid any brand that only does sticker assembly – their NAND sources are unknown, and the drive may fail at any moment. OEM vs. Retail Drives OEM and retail drives are identical hardware. Retail drives come with official warranty and driver support; OEM drives are warrantied through the channel vendor at a lower price. OEM drives are typically sourced through secondary channels – always verify the seller's warranty terms before purchase. Personal Recommendations (for reference only) My first recommendation is original SSDs, e.g., ZhiTai TiPro 9000. Among OEM drives, the following three are worth considering: PVC10 (SK hynix) PCB01 (SK hynix) AM6C1 (UnionMemory, under UMIS) Avoid Samsung PM9A1 and any model known for "0e" errors (uncorrectable data corruption leading to permanent data loss). Also avoid any white‑label, gray‑label, or no‑name SSDs. Your storage drive holds all your important data – essays, photos, code, game saves. A low‑quality drive may die suddenly, and data recovery is expensive and not guaranteed. Saving a few dollars is not worth that risk. Considerations for Adding an SSD to a Laptop Before adding an SSD to your laptop, check the following: Empty M.2 slot: search for motherboard photos or disassembly videos of your model. The second slot on some laptops may only support short drives (2242 or 2230); installing a 2280 drive may not fit. M.2 form factors: common lengths are 2230 (30mm), 2242 (42mm), and 2280 (80mm). 2280 is the most common. For 2242, the PVC10 and PC411 are worthwhile choices. Power consumption and drop‑out risk: laptops have far less power delivery and cooling than desktops. Verify the drive's sustained power consumption – a high‑power drive can overheat and disconnect in a thin‑and‑light. Recommended reviewers: Bilibili creators "前进的四火" and "HOMOLAB" produce high‑quality SSD reviews – they use professional tools like fio for steady‑state testing, not just peak speeds. Current timing: SSD prices are high in 2026 – if not urgent, wait for prices to drop. Extended 6: Display Selection Display preference is subjective – I strongly recommend visiting a physical store to compare different panels with your own eyes. Personal preference Some users prefer high‑quality LCD panels (especially IPS or MiniLED backlit) because LCD has no OLED burn‑in risk, higher full‑screen brightness, and sharper text. Resolution vs. Refresh Rate Compared to high refresh rates (e.g., 120Hz), high resolution (e.g., 2560×1600 or 3840×2160) delivers crisper text and images, significantly improving productivity for office work, coding, and reading. 60Hz is sufficient for non‑competitive gaming. When budget is limited, prioritising resolution is a reasonable choice. Color Accuracy and Gamut Coverage Color accuracy (measured by Delta E) and gamut coverage are equally important. Color accuracy affects your judgement of colours – for example, you take a photo with your phone, edit it in Lightroom on your laptop; if the display is inaccurate, the colours you adjust may look completely wrong to others. Even for casual photo editing or watching movies, you want colours to be reasonably true. Gamut coverage determines how many colours the display can show – common standards include sRGB, DCI‑P3, etc. For most users, covering 100% sRGB is the baseline. Factory Calibration and Calibrators Modern thin‑and‑light laptops generally have decent out‑of‑box colour accuracy, but do not blindly trust "factory calibrated" claims. Factory calibration is often done on a few samples, and the reported Delta E is measured under specific brightness and mode – it does not guarantee your unit is the same. If you truly demand high colour accuracy (note: if you do not know what "colour accuracy" means, you probably do not need it for the foreseeable future), the most reliable method is to rent a colorimeter (e.g., Spyder or Calibrite) and calibrate your screen following a tutorial. Generate and load an ICC profile. Calibrate once a year. Extended 7: Buying Principles for Gaming and All‑rounder Laptops For gaming laptops, a common core principle is: given acceptable performance release and a decent display, choose the cheapest one. Different brands with the same CPU/GPU can have vastly different sustained power limits (i.e., performance release). Check real cooling and stress tests from reviewers like 笔吧评测室. Only after confirming that performance release is not crippled should you compare prices. For all‑rounder laptops, trying them in person is recommended – chassis thickness, cooling, and fan noise vary greatly between models.

title: SystemTuningANDAntimalware
content: Appendix 2: System Tuning and Antimalware This chapter covers only the most essential maintenance principles and operations. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section that follows. 2.1 Core Principle: If You Don‘t Understand It, Don't Touch It The default configuration of Windows has been thoroughly tested and works well for the vast majority of use cases. Many online "optimisation" guides tell you to disable certain system services to free up memory, but this often breaks features you may need later (e.g., disabling the print spooler makes printers unusable), and you are unlikely to remember that you disabled it. The only safe rule: if you do not know exactly what a setting does, do not change it. Using your computer normally without blindly tweaking settings is the best optimisation. 2.2 Antimalware: The Built‑In One Is Good Enough Windows comes with Microsoft Defender Antimalware, which is more than sufficient for most personal users. Its signatures update frequently, it integrates deeply with the system, and it does not consume excessive resources. For the vast majority of people, no third‑party antimalware is needed. 2.3 Handling Third‑Party Security Software 2.3.1 Chinese Security Suites: Generally Not Needed Software such as 360, Tencent PC Manager, and Kingsoft Antivirus is usually not recommended. They often bring pop‑up ads, bundled promotions, consume background resources, and may even have security vulnerabilities of their own. 2.3.2 Pre‑installed McAfee: Recommended to Uninstall Many branded laptops (e.g., some Asus and Dell models) come with a pre‑installed McAfee trial, often including a two‑year license. Given that McAfee has had security vulnerabilities in the past and runs at the kernel driver level, issues can be serious. It is advisable to uninstall it. Search for "McAfee Consumer Product Removal tool" – run it to cleanly remove everything. 2.4 Manufacturer Pre‑installed Software: Keep Only the Control Centre Branded laptops come with various pre‑installed software. The only thing worth keeping is the hardware control centre, for example: Lenovo Vantage (Lenovo) Armoury Crate (Asus) Dell Power Manager (Dell) These tools let you adjust performance modes, fan speeds, battery charge thresholds, etc. All other pre‑installed software (e.g., AI assistants, music players, app store promotions, trial software) can be safely uninstalled. 2.5 Do Not Fill Up Your C: Drive (The Most Important Optimisation) Keep at least 20% free space on your C: drive (i.e., usage below 80%). If the C: drive runs out of space, your computer will become noticeably slow, because Windows uses the hard drive as temporary memory (swap). Once your C: drive gets close to full, immediately clean up unnecessary files or move your user folders (Documents, Downloads, Desktop, etc.) to another drive. Search online for "how to change the location of user folders in Windows" for instructions. 2.6 Good Habits Are the Best Security Measure Download software only from official websites or the Microsoft Store. Do not click random pop‑up ads, especially those claiming "Your computer is infected". Do not plug in unknown USB drives without caution. When installing any software, do not blindly click "Next" repeatedly. Slow down and check each step for options such as "install XX browser", "set as homepage", or "install to the C: drive" (you may prefer D:). Uncheck any options you do not need. Once you develop these habits, Microsoft Defender will handle the remaining security risks adequately. 2.7 First Steps After You First Boot into the System After connecting to the internet, go to Settings → Windows Update → "Check for updates". Install all available updates (may require several restarts). Go to Settings → Apps, and uninstall unnecessary pre‑installed software (including McAfee). Restart your PC. In the system tray, confirm that the Microsoft Defender shield icon is present and healthy. 2.8 Windows Update: Do Not Disable It Many old tutorials suggest "disabling Windows Update" because it consumes bandwidth or may restart your computer. That advice no longer applies today. Windows Update does far more than just fixing security holes. It also: Automatically updates many Microsoft applications, such as Office suites and runtimes. Updates hardware drivers (graphics, network, audio, etc.), preventing blue screens or performance issues caused by outdated drivers. Updates Windows Defender's virus definitions, keeping your computer protected against the latest threats. If you worry about sudden reboots interrupting your work, do this instead: Go to Settings → Windows Update → Advanced options → Active hours. Set the time period when you normally use your computer (e.g., 09:00 to 18:00). Windows will not automatically restart during those hours. Outside active hours, if a restart is required for an update, Windows will do it when idle, or you can manually choose a restart time. Not updating Windows does NOT make your system more stable. On the contrary, skipping updates for a long time accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities and driver bugs, which may lead to blue screens, sluggishness, or even malware attacks. Leave automatic updates on, configure active hours properly – that is the smarter approach. Extended Reading The following sections contain detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the must‑read part. Extended 1: Why You Should Not Mess with the Registry and Group Policy The Registry is Windows's configuration database, storing almost every setting for hardware, software, and users. Group Policy is a graphical interface for configuring the Registry in bulk. Incorrect modifications can render the system unbootable or break features permanently. For example, someone disabled the Print Spooler to "save memory", and months later could not print – it took them a long time to realise they had turned it off. If you do not know what these tools are, stay away from them entirely. Extended 2: Microsoft Defender vs. Common Chinese Security Suites Microsoft Defender has no ads, no pop‑ups, does not collect personal usage data, and uses few resources. By contrast, Chinese security suites (e.g., 360, Tencent PC Manager) offer extra gadgets (software updaters, network speed tests) but at the cost of frequent ad pop‑ups, bundled installs, and background data uploads. In major international security tests, Microsoft Defender consistently ranks in the top tier. For non‑high‑risk personal use, Defender is the safer choice. Extended 3: How to Uninstall McAfee Properly McAfee is recommended for removal not only because of past security vulnerabilities (e.g., remote code execution), but also because it is notoriously difficult to uninstall fully – normal "Add/Remove Programs" often leaves behind drivers and services. Use the official "McAfee Consumer Product Removal" from McAfee's website. Run it to automatically detect and clean everything. If your laptop is brand new and you haven't activated McAfee yet, uninstalling from Settings is cleaner and leaves fewer traces. Extended 4: Categorising Manufacturer Pre‑installed Software Must keep: Hardware control centre (performance modes, fans, battery thresholds). Without it, you may lose the ability to adjust screen brightness, keyboard backlight, or set charge limits. Safe to remove: "AI assistants", "PC manager", app store promotions, music/video trials, cloud storage promotions – most are third‑party customisations with mediocre experience and resource usage. Optional: Driver update utilities from the manufacturer (e.g., Lenovo Driver Manager). If you can download drivers from the official website yourself, you can remove these as well. Extended 5: Swap (Virtual Memory) Explained Operating systems use a mechanism called swap (or page file). When physical RAM is insufficient, the system moves some temporarily unused data from RAM to a file on the hard drive (pagefile.sys), freeing RAM for active programs. Even when physical RAM is abundant, Windows may pre‑swap some data to optimise memory layout. This page file resides on the C: drive by default. If the C: drive has very little free space, the page file cannot expand properly, or the free space is fragmented. The system then constantly reads and writes to the hard drive for swapping, making the computer extremely slow. This is why a full C: drive is disastrous. Extended 6: SLC Cache and Write Principles on SSDs Most consumer SSDs use TLC (3 bits per cell) or QLC (4 bits per cell) NAND. To boost write speed, the SSD internally reserves a portion as SLC cache (1 bit per cell, fast writing). When the amount of data written exceeds the cache size, the drive switches to TLC/QLC direct write mode, and speed drops dramatically. When SSD usage exceeds roughly 60%, the controller gradually reduces or even disables the SLC cache, forcing TLC direct write. Worse, the remaining free space is often not a single contiguous area – it is scattered with logical traces of deleted files. Writing new data then requires the SSD to read the existing block, modify it in memory, and write it back (read‑modify‑write). This further reduces performance and increases write amplification, shortening the drive's lifespan. Therefore, keeping your C: drive sufficiently free is not only for virtual memory but also to maintain the SSD's high‑speed writing capability. Extended 7: Malware‑Patch and Similar Tools Malware‑Patch is a small open‑source tool (project page: https://github.com/the1812/Malware-Patch). It does not actively scan for malware; instead, it uses UAC (User Account Control – the pop‑up that asks for permission when installing software) to intercept installation attempts by common unwanted software. When you double‑click on certain "family bucket" installers, it shows a warning. For beginners, this is a mild aid, but it is not essential. If you already have the habit of downloading software only from official sources, you do not need it. Extended 8: On "Make Your PC Fly" Optimisation Videos Many online videos claim that a few registry tweaks can dramatically boost performance. Most such "optimisations" are either placebo, trade stability for a tiny gain, or even disable important security mechanisms. The only real ways to keep a computer running smoothly are: Keep enough free space on your C: drive. Ensure proper cooling (clean dust, elevate the laptop). Do not install software that noticeably slows down the system (e.g., certain antimalware suites). For everything else, Windows manages memory and background processes on its own. Trust the default configuration and spend your time on real work and entertainment – that is the best optimisation. Extended 9: The Myth of "Disabling Windows Update" There was once a popular belief that disabling Windows Update improves performance and avoids forced restarts. This stemmed from the poor update experience and lack of restart control in early Windows versions (like Windows 7/8). Since Windows 10, Microsoft has significantly improved the update mechanism: Most updates download silently in the background, consuming little to no foreground resources. The "Active hours" feature gives users reasonable control. Driver updates are delivered through Windows Update, saving users the trouble of hunting for drivers themselves. In fact, many issues on long‑unupdated computers (random blue screens, inability to install new software, peripheral incompatibility, etc.) often disappear automatically after installing all Windows and driver updates. Therefore, keeping Windows Update enabled and checking it regularly is one of the simplest and most effective ways to maintain a healthy system.

title: FileManagement
content: Turn Off BitLocker Turn Off BitLocker Turn Off BitLocker The very first thing you do after getting a new laptop: turn off BitLocker. BitLocker is Windows's full‑disk encryption feature. It encrypts your drive, and only a recovery key can unlock it. That sounds secure, but for individual users, the downsides heavily outweigh any benefit: You will almost never need it. BitLocker is designed for corporate or government scenarios where a lost device might leak sensitive data. The chance of losing your personal laptop is tiny, and your data is not that valuable to an attacker. If your system crashes, the motherboard fails, or you lose the recovery key, all your data is gone forever. Microsoft will not help you decrypt it. It slightly reduces drive performance, especially for small file reads and writes. Your data is priceless. I strongly suggest you turn BitLocker off to avoid the risk of permanent data loss. How to check and disable it: Open Settings → Privacy & security → Device encryption (or search for "BitLocker"). If it says "Off", you are fine. If it says "On", open PowerShell or Command Prompt as Administrator and run: Wait for decryption to complete. You can check progress with in the same terminal. Decryption may take from a few tens of minutes to hours. You can use your computer normally during this time, but keep it plugged in and powered on until done. Ignore anyone who tells you to "keep BitLocker". For you, turning it off is the smarter choice. Appendix 3: File Management and Storage Philosophy This chapter covers only the most essential file management and storage operations. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section. 3.1 Partition Your Drive: Separate C: and D: New computers usually come with a single C: drive. Putting everything (system, documents, downloads) on C: means that if the system crashes and you need to reinstall Windows, all your data is lost. So it is wise to split the drive into two partitions. Example: Your laptop has a 1TB SSD. You can leave 300GB for C: and use the remaining ~650GB for D:. C: drive (system): Only Windows, drivers, and a few programs that must be on C: (e.g., certain development tools). Nothing else. D: drive (data): Your documents, photos, videos, downloaded installers, Steam library, project code, etc. Why do this? If Windows breaks and you have to reinstall, you only need to format C:. Everything on D: remains untouched. After reinstalling Steam, you can add the D: Steam library folder in settings – no need to redownload games. How to do it: Use the built‑in Disk Management (right‑click "This PC" → Manage → Disk Management). Right‑click C: and choose "Shrink Volume" to free up space, then create a new simple volume with the free space and assign it drive letter D:. If unsure, search for "how to partition laptop drive" on YouTube and follow a recent tutorial. 3.2 Organise Files with Numbered Prefixes Do not just pile folders directly on D:. It is much better to use a category + number scheme. For example: 01Work: Internships, part‑time jobs, student club documents. 02Study: Course materials, papers, eBooks. 03Media: Personal photos, music, movies. 04Downloads: Browser cache. Clean it once a week or month – move useful files to other folders, delete the rest. 05_Archive: Things you no longer use but cannot bear to delete (e.g., old versions of your graduation project). Why the number prefix? Windows sorts by character order. appears before , so your most important folders are always the first you see when you open D:. 3.3 Game Storage: Delete When Done, Keep Cloud Saves Games on Steam and Epic are now huge (50–100GB). You usually play only two or three at a time. Games you have finished and will never touch again just waste space. My approach: Keep only the games you are actively playing. When you finish a game (or know you will not touch it for a while), first make sure your cloud saves are synchronised (Steam does this by default), then uninstall it from Steam. When you want to replay it, just download it again. 3.4 Backup Strategy: The 3‑2‑1 Rule (Simplified) The 3‑2‑1 rule is a basic consensus in data protection: 3 copies of your data (original + two backups) 2 different storage media (e.g., internal SSD + external hard drive) 1 off‑site copy (e.g., cloud storage) For students, you can simplify: Original data: On your laptop D: drive. Local backup: Every two weeks or every month, copy your most important folders (documents, photos, code projects) to an external hard drive. Off‑site backup: Use a cloud service like Baidu Netdisk, OneDrive, or Aliyun Drive to sync a copy of your important files. Never use a no‑name USB flash drive as your only backup! Cheap drives can die after just a few uses. If you need a flash drive, buy a reputable brand (e.g., SanDisk CZ74). For more details on hard drive selection and backup, see the Extended Reading section. 3.5 Simple Cloud Storage Choices If possible, prefer international services: OneDrive (the 1TB that comes with Office 365), Google Drive, Dropbox. Their clients are stable and they treat privacy somewhat better. Chinese alternatives: Baidu Netdisk (speed limited but usable for incremental backup), Aliyun Drive (currently less throttling). Highly sensitive data (e.g., ID card scans, password backups): Never upload them directly to any cloud. Use an open‑source encryption tool like VeraCrypt or a password‑protected AES‑256 7‑Zip archive, then upload the encrypted file. 3.6 Keep Your Computer Clock Accurate: Change the NTP Server If your computer clock is often wrong (e.g., a few minutes slow after boot), it is because Windows's default time server is overseas and has high latency. Manual sync steps: Right‑click the clock on the taskbar → "Adjust date/time". Under "Synchronise your clock", click "Sync now".
