Markdown is a lightweight markup language that lets you write documents in plain text and then convert them to clean, formatted HTML. It is much simpler than Word and much nicer to look at than Notepad. This appendix covers only the most basic syntax. For more detailed tutorials, please visit . 13.1 What Is Markdown? Markdown is a plain‑text markup language. Instead of using your mouse to click a "bold" button, you just add a few symbols around your text. For example: Markdown files usually have the extension. You can open and edit them with any text editor (Notepad, VS Code). After writing, you can convert the file to HTML, PDF, Word, or other formats. What can you do with Markdown? Write README files (the project descriptions you see on GitHub are almost all Markdown) Write blog posts (many static blog systems such as Hexo, Hugo, and VuePress use Markdown) Take notes (Obsidian, Typora, and Notion all support Markdown) Write technical documentation (many open source projects use Markdown for their docs) In fact, all the content of this site was written in Markdown Markdown's biggest feature is that it is plain text – you can open it on any computer without worrying about layout breaking, unlike files. The syntax is extremely simple; you can learn it in ten minutes. 13.2 Basic Syntax Below is the most commonly used Markdown syntax. For a more complete reference, see the "Basic Syntax" section on markdown.com.cn. 13.2.1 Headings Use to indicate a heading. The number of symbols indicates the heading level. Always put a space after the . 13.2.2 Paragraphs and Line Breaks Separate paragraphs with a blank line. If you only want a line break (without starting a new paragraph), add two spaces at the end of the line, then press Enter. 13.2.3 Emphasis 13.2.4 Lists Unordered lists: Use , , or , followed by a space. Ordered lists: Use a number followed by a period, then a space. The numbers do not have to be sequential – Markdown will renumber them automatically. 13.2.5 Links 13.2.6 Images 13.2.7 Blockquotes Use to indicate a blockquote. You can nest them ( ). 13.2.8 Code Inline code: Wrap the code with backticks (the key above Tab, to the left of ). Code blocks: Wrap the code with three backticks. You can specify a language for syntax highlighting. ~markdown ~ 13.2.9 Horizontal Rules Use three or more , , or on a line by themselves. 13.2.10 Tables Use to separate cells and to separate the header from the body. 13.2.11 Task Lists Use for incomplete tasks and for completed tasks. 13.3 Extended Syntax Standard Markdown is fairly basic. Extended syntax adds more useful features: strikethrough, automatic links, footnotes, definition lists, Emoji, highlighting, subscripts, superscripts, and more. However, not all Markdown renderers support extended syntax. Examples of common extended syntax: For a detailed explanation of extended syntax, see the "Extended Syntax" section on . 13.4 What Tools Can You Use? VS Code: Install the extension. You can preview, generate tables of contents, and export to HTML. Typora: A dedicated Markdown editor that is "what you see is what you get" – you type the syntax, and it shows the rendered result in real time. Clean interface, good for beginners. Obsidian: A knowledge management tool that supports Markdown. Great for building a personal note archive. Any text editor: Even Notepad works, though you will not get preview. 13.5 A Final Thought Markdown is not a replacement for Word – for complex layouts, exact margins, or academic references, you should still use Word or LaTeX. But for everyday notes, documents, READMEs, and blog posts, Markdown is the most hassle‑free way to write. You do not need to memorise all the syntax. Just remember for headings, for bold, , and . That is enough. Look up the rest when you need it.

title: Color
content: Appendix 14: Color This appendix introduces the basic concepts of color – gamut, color space, color accuracy, and calibration. If you only use your computer to watch videos, play games, and edit your own photos, you probably won't need this knowledge. But if you start doing design work, photo retouching, or video editing, and need to share your work with others or send it to print, understanding these concepts will help. 14.1 The Most Important Thing You Need to Know If you are not delivering final work to someone else (e.g., sending to a client, printing, submitting to a publication) – if you are just using your computer for games, watching videos, or editing your own photos – then whether your screen's colors are "accurate" simply does not matter. Use whatever looks comfortable to you. Color management is a rabbit hole. Unless you make a living from color (graphic design, retouching, video color grading, printing), you do not need to go deep. If you ever need it later, just knowing that it exists and knowing which direction to search is enough. 14.2 Gamut and Color Space 14.2.1 What Is Gamut? Gamut is the range of colors that a device (a monitor, printer, projector) or a color standard can reproduce. The human eye can see many colors, but different devices can only cover a portion of them. Common gamut standards: | Gamut | Coverage (relative to human vision) | Main use | One‑sentence explanation | |-------|--------------------------------------|----------|---------------------------| | sRGB | About 35% | Web, ordinary monitors, Windows default | The most universal "safe" gamut. Almost every device displays it correctly. | | DCI-P3 | About 45% | Digital cinema, Apple devices, HDR video | Wider than sRGB, especially in reds and greens. | | Display P3 | About 45% | Apple displays | Based on DCI-P3, but with the same white point as sRGB for better compatibility. | | Adobe RGB | About 50% | Professional photography, printing | Enhanced cyan and green to cover the CMYK print gamut. | | Rec. 709 | Almost identical to sRGB | HDTV | sRGB's "TV version" – slightly different white point and gamma. | | Rec. 2020 | About 75% | 4K/8K UHDTV | One of the widest gamuts available; almost no consumer display can fully cover it. | 14.2.2 Three Names, Essentially the Same Range sRGB, Rec.709, and Rec.601 have nearly identical color ranges. The differences: sRGB: For computer monitors, the web, consumer digital cameras Rec.709: For HDTV – white point is the same as sRGB, gamma curve is slightly different Rec.601: Standard for SDTV, now largely replaced by Rec.709 For ordinary users, you can treat them as the same thing – the "common small gamut". The vast majority of images and videos you see online are in sRGB or Rec.709. 14.2.3 OKLAB: Why It Exists Traditional color spaces like sRGB and P3 are not mathematically "uniform". What does that mean? In sRGB, a numeric change of 10 might look large in dark areas but barely noticeable in bright areas. OKLAB is a newer color model designed so that the same numeric change produces the same perceptual change for the human eye. OKLAB is mainly used inside color conversion algorithms (for example, converting an sRGB image to P3 without introducing a color cast). Ordinary users do not need to work with it directly, but you can remember: if you see a piece of software that supports OKLAB, it handles color more scientifically. 14.2.4 Why So Many Gamuts? Different industries have different needs. Printing requires coverage of CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow, black), hence Adobe RGB. Cinema needs a wider dynamic range and vivid reds/greens, hence DCI-P3. Television has evolved from SDTV to HDTV to UHDTV, giving us Rec.601, Rec.709, and Rec.2020. For ordinary users, sRGB is the safest. If you create a very vivid image on a wide‑gamut monitor and send it to a friend who uses a normal sRGB monitor, they will see less saturated colors. Conversely, when someone sends you an sRGB image and you view it on a wide‑gamut monitor without proper color management, the colors will be incorrectly "stretched" and look oversaturated. This is why many designers switch their monitors to sRGB mode when editing. 14.3 Monitor Gamut Coverage When buying a monitor, you will see specs like "99% sRGB coverage" or "95% DCI-P3 coverage". What do these numbers mean? Gamut coverage: What percentage of a given gamut this monitor can actually display. 99% sRGB means the monitor can show 99% of the colors inside the sRGB triangle; the remaining 1% cannot be shown. Gamut volume: The ratio of the monitor's total color area to the area of a reference gamut. It is possible to have "120% sRGB volume" – but that does not mean accurate color, because the extra 20% may be in entirely wrong directions. For ordinary users: A monitor that covers 100% sRGB is already very good for daily use. Wider gamuts (P3, Adobe RGB) are not necessary unless you have a specific need (e.g., editing HDR video, doing print design). 14.4 Color Accuracy: ΔE (Delta E) ΔE (Delta E) is a number that measures how "accurate" a color is. The smaller the ΔE, the smaller the difference between the displayed color and the standard reference color. | ΔE range | Meaning | |----------|---------| | ΔE 5 | Color cast is clearly visible to the naked eye | Monitor ΔE values are usually quoted as "average ΔE". For example, "average ΔE < 2" means most colors are fairly accurate, but some colors (e.g., deep blue) may be off by more. For ordinary users: Do not obsess over ΔE. When you are gaming, you do not care whether "this red is the exact sRGB red". As long as colors are not wildly wrong (e.g., white looking pink), you are fine. 14.5 Calibration Devices and Calibration If you truly need accurate color (for example, you have taken a design job and the client requires no color deviation), then you need calibration. 14.5.1 What Is a Calibration Device? A colorimeter (or spectrophotometer) is a small, mouse‑sized piece of hardware. You attach it to your screen, it measures the colors your screen actually displays, and then it generates an ICC profile for your operating system. Once Windows loads this profile, it adjusts the output signal to make the screen more accurate. Common calibration device brands: Datacolor Spyder: Common models include Spyder X, Spyder 5. Suitable for ordinary users and photography enthusiasts. Calibrite (formerly X-Rite) : More professional – e.g., ColorChecker Display, i1Display Pro. Many studios use these. 14.5.2 Calibration Steps Connect the calibration device to your computer and install the accompanying software (or use the open‑source DisplayCAL). Let your monitor warm up for at least 30 minutes (so colors stabilise). In the software, set your targets: white point (usually D65, i.e., 6500K), brightness (120 cd/m² for a typical indoor environment), gamma (choose 2.2 for sRGB/Rec.709). Attach the device to the center of your screen and run the measurement. The software will display a series of colors, and the device reads them one by one. When the measurement finishes, the software generates an ICC profile and tells Windows to load it. Take this with a grain of salt – I researched this information; I have never used one myself. If you really need calibration, it is best to ask the vendor for advice. 14.5.3 When Do You Need Calibration? You just bought a new monitor: Factory calibration is not always accurate, and it drifts over time. Professional users calibrate every 1–2 months. You changed your graphics card or reinstalled your OS: The system's color configuration may have been lost. You notice two screens look different: For example, your laptop screen and an external monitor clearly do not match. You are sending work to print: Printing has strict color requirements. Without calibration, the printed result may be wildly off. 14.5.4 When Do You NOT Need Calibration? You only game and watch videos: Not needed. You use a built‑in laptop screen: The hardware quality of laptop screens is limited. Calibration will not improve it much, and it is not worth the expense. You occasionally edit photos, only to post on social media: Not needed. No one on social media is comparing your photos against a color checker. You do not own a calibration device: You can rent one (available on platforms like Taobao for a few dozen RMB per day) or borrow from a friend. Buying one costs anywhere from a few hundred to over a thousand RMB – if you only need it once, renting is more economical. 14.6 When Color Management Is Important vs. When It Is Not 14.6.1 When You Must Take Color Management Seriously Design work delivered to a client: If a blue that looks great on your screen looks purple on the client's screen, your final payment may be at risk. Printing: A screen and a piece of paper are completely different media. Without color management, the printed output will look nothing like what you see on screen. Video color grading delivered to a platform (Bilibili, YouTube, etc.) : If you set the wrong color space, the platform will re‑encode the video and the colors will shift. Product photography (Taobao, e‑commerce) : If the color of a garment is inaccurate, customers will receive items that look different from the photos, leading to high return rates. 14.6.2 When You Can Ignore Color Management Playing games: Not needed. Watching videos and movies: Not needed. The video is already graded; you are seeing what the director intended (as long as your monitor is not terrible). Editing your own photos, only to post on social media or keep on your phone: Not needed. Your friends use different brands of phones, each with different screen colors – no matter how accurately you calibrate, the colors will look different on their screens. Relax. Coding, writing documents, taking online classes: Color has nothing to do with the content. Not needed. 14.6.3 One‑Sentence Summary If you are not delivering work to others – if it is just for your own enjoyment – do not bother with color management. Spending your energy on content is far more valuable than spending it on color accuracy. 14.7 Windows Color Management: Why It Is More Complicated Than on Mac Let me briefly explain this. Many people say "Mac colors are accurate, Windows colors are a mess". The reason lies in the different designs of the two systems: macOS: System‑level, mandatory color management. Regardless of the application (even old software that does not support color management), macOS maps color data to the display's actual gamut at the system level. Combined with Apple's factory‑calibrated screens, it is accurate out of the box. Windows: Applications are on their own. Programs that support color management (Photoshop, Lightroom, Chrome/Edge) handle colors correctly. Programs that do not support it (older games, old screenshot tools, some image viewers) simply send their color values directly to the screen. If you have a wide‑gamut screen, colors in those applications will appear oversaturated. This difference does not affect ordinary users. But if you need accurate color and do not want to tinker, a Mac is indeed the more hassle‑free choice. Extended Reading The following sections involve mathematical calculations and deeper principles of color spaces. They are more advanced. Skim them first, and come back later when you need them. Extended 1: The CIE 1931 Chromaticity Diagram In 1931, the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) defined the CIE 1931 XYZ color space, which forms the foundation of all modern colorimetry. It is a horseshoe‑shaped diagram of human color perception. The x and y axes represent chromaticity (color, without brightness). Any gamut can be drawn as a triangle inside this horseshoe – the three vertices are the coordinates of that gamut's red, green, and blue primaries. sRGB, DCI-P3, and Rec.2020 are all different‑sized triangles inside this horseshoe. Extended 2: Gamut Coverage vs. Gamut Volume – The Mathematical Difference Coverage: The area of overlap between the monitor's gamut and the reference gamut, divided by the area of the reference gamut (a percentage). Coverage cannot exceed 100%. Volume: The total area of the monitor's gamut divided by the area of the reference gamut (a percentage). Volume can exceed 100% (meaning the monitor's gamut is wider than the reference). A monitor might claim "120% sRGB volume", but if that extra 20% volume lies in wrong directions, the monitor may still be inaccurate when displaying sRGB content. High volume does not necessarily mean good – coverage is a better indicator of accuracy for a given gamut. Extended 3: CIE Lab vs. OKLAB CIE Lab (also called CIELAB, Lab) is a color space defined by the CIE in 1976. It was designed to be "perceptually uniform" – but later research found that it is still not very uniform, especially in the blue region. OKLAB (proposed in 2020) improves uniformity, particularly in blue and cyan areas. OKLAB is currently one of the better color spaces for color conversion algorithms (e.g., converting from P3 to sRGB). Adobe Photoshop, Blender, and OpenColorIO have started to support OKLAB. Extended 4: White Point and Color Temperature The white point determines the coordinates of "white" on the chromaticity diagram. Common white points: D65: 6500K, corresponds to midday sunlight. sRGB, Rec.709, and Display P3 all use D65. D50: 5000K, slightly yellowish. The standard for the printing industry (because printing paper itself is not pure white). Original DCI-P3 white point: 6300K, slightly different from D65. Display P3 changed the white point to D65 for better compatibility with sRGB. Color temperature is measured in Kelvin (K). Lower values look more yellow/red (warm), higher values look more blue (cool). The "warm", "standard", and "cool" settings on a TV adjust the white point. Extended 5: How Calibration Data Is Stored The ICC profile generated by a calibration device is a file containing a CLUT (Color Lookup Table) . When Windows loads this profile, the graphics card applies the table when outputting signals: . This process requires GPU and OS support. Some older games may bypass color management entirely, making the calibration ineffective. Extended 6: Using a Wide‑Gamut Monitor for Everyday Work If you have bought a wide‑gamut monitor (e.g., covering 95% DCI-P3) but mainly use Windows, here is some advice: Switch your monitor to sRGB mode** via its on‑screen display (OSD) menu. This makes the monitor internally compress the wide gamut down to sRGB, so all applications (including those that do not support color management) show correct colors. If you truly need the wide gamut (e.g., for editing HDR video), enable color management inside your editing software, but switch back to sRGB mode for everyday use. Alternatively, only enable wide‑gamut mode when you are certain you need it. Use sRGB mode the rest of the time – no fuss.

title: 音视频
content: 附录十五：音视频 这个附录介绍音视频处理的基本概念和常用工具。包括编解码器、容器格式、码率、OBS 录屏设置，以及剪辑软件的选择。后面的补充阅读留给 FFmpeg 命令行用法和更深入的技术概念。 15.1 编解码器（Codec） 编码器（Encoder） 把原始音视频数据压缩成某种格式。解码器（Decoder） 把压缩后的数据还原成可以播放的信号。 15.1.1 视频编解码器 | 名称 | 常见编码器 | 一句话说明 | |------|-----------|------------| | H.264 / AVC | （软件）、 （N卡）、 （Intel核显） | 兼容性最好，几乎所有设备都能播。 | | H.265 / HEVC | （软件）、 （N卡）、 （Intel核显） | 同等画质下文件比 H.264 小。 | | AV1 | 、 （软件） | 压缩率更高，适合在线流媒体。 | 提醒： 需要 NVIDIA 显卡， 需要 Intel 核显。不是所有电脑都有。 软件编码 vs 硬件编码： 软件编码（ 、 、 ）：画质好、体积小，但吃 CPU，速度慢。适合精压制片、存档。 硬件编码（ 、 ）：速度快（比软件快 5-10 倍），但同等码率下画质稍差。适合录屏、直播、快速导出。 15.1.2 音频编解码器 | 名称 | 常见编码器 | 一句话说明 | |------|-----------|------------| | AAC | | 目前最通用的音频格式，几乎所有视频都用它。 | | MP3 | | 老格式，兼容性好，但同码率下音质不如 AAC。 | | FLAC | | 无损压缩，体积大，适合存档、听歌。 | | Opus | | 新技术，音质好压缩率高，部分老设备不支持。 | 15.2 容器格式（Container） 容器格式 是装视频、音频、字幕的“盒子”。同一个 H.265 编码的视频，可以放进 ，也可以放进 。 | 容器 | 特点 | |------|------| | MP4 | 最通用，几乎所有设备都能播。缺点：通常只能装一条视频、一条音轨、一条字幕。 | | MKV | 功能强大，可以装多音轨、多字幕、章节信息。损坏后恢复能力强（只有最后几秒坏掉）。 | | MOV | 苹果的 QuickTime 格式，也支持多轨道。适合在苹果设备和 Windows 之间交换。 | 15.3 码率（Bitrate） 码率是视频每秒的数据量，单位 kbps（千比特每秒）或 Mbps（兆比特每秒）。码率越高，画质越好，文件越大。 CBR（固定码率）：从头到尾码率不变。适合直播。 VBR（可变码率）：简单画面给低码率，复杂画面给高码率。同等平均码率下画质更好。 CRF（恒定质量）：编码器自动分配码率，保证每一帧的质量大致相同。日常压制最省心。 15.4 OBS 录屏设置 15.4.1 基础设置 输出模式：高级 → 输出设为“输出到文件” 容器格式：选 MKV（原因：如果录制过程中软件崩溃或断电，MKV 只会损坏最后几秒；MP4 会全坏） 编码器： 有 Intel 核显 + 独显 → 选 QuickSync HEVC（用核显编码，不占用独显资源，对游戏帧数影响最小） 只有 N 卡 → 选 NVENC HEVC 只有 A 卡 → 选 AMD AMF HEVC（祝你好运） 15.4.2 参数建议 | 分辨率 | 码率 | 帧率 | 关键帧间隔 | B 帧 | |--------|------|------|------------|------| | 1080p | 35 Mbps | 60 fps | 3 秒 | 3 | | 4K | 90 Mbps | 60 fps | 3 秒 | 3 | 游戏画面没有动态模糊，每一帧都是瞬间截图，快速移动时细节容易崩。所以游戏录制的码率要比普通视频高。 关于 B 帧：B 帧（双向预测帧）可以提高压缩率，但会增加编码延迟。设为 3 是在画质和兼容性之间的平衡。 15.4.3 管理员权限 对于某些全屏游戏，如果 OBS 捕获不到画面，请右键以管理员身份运行 OBS。 15.5 剪辑软件 15.5.1 Adobe 全家桶 Premiere Pro：剪辑，行业标准之一。 After Effects：特效、合成、动态图形。 Audition：音频编辑、降噪、混音。 Adobe 软件是订阅制的。你可以从 Creative Cloud 下载试用版后，不要打开软件，立刻运行 Adobe GenP 激活。我不提供下载。具体步骤请自行搜索 GitHub 或相关论坛。这涉及到版权问题，请自行判断。 15.5.2 DaVinci Resolve Blackmagic Design 出品的专业剪辑调色软件。免费版已经非常强大——剪辑、调色（好莱坞电影在用）、Fairlight 音频、Fusion 特效全流程整合。对色彩要求高的情况下，这款比 Premiere 更合适。 15.5.3 开源替代 如果你不想花钱，也不想折腾盗版，下面这三个开源软件值得一试： Clypra Clypra 是一款基于 Tauri + React + TypeScript + Rust + FFmpeg 构建的现代开源视频编辑器，采用 MIT 许可证。目标是免费复刻剪映国际版（CapCut）的付费功能。它没有使用 Electron（资源占用高），因此启动速度和内存占用都比同类工具有优势。 核心功能： 多轨道专业时间轴，支持拖拽剪辑、帧级精确裁剪 实时音频波形显示，方便卡点 胶片预览条（Filmstrip），通过缩略图快速定位内容 文字字幕与标题，支持自定义字体 项目管理与自动保存，100 级撤销/重做 支持 MP4、MOV、MKV、AVI 等视频格式，MP3、WAV、AAC 等音频格式 跨平台：Windows、macOS、Linux 尚未实现：AI 自动字幕、特效转场库、色彩分级、绿幕去背（开发中）。 适合谁：短视频创作者、自媒体新手、不想付费给剪映的人。基础剪辑已经够用。 官网：GitHub 搜索 Audacity Audacity 是一款历史悠久、易于上手的开源多轨音频编辑器和录音软件，基于 GPLv3 许可证，支持 Windows、macOS、Linux。 核心功能： 多轨编辑，支持无限轨道 导入导出 WAV、AIFF、MP3、OGG、FLAC 等主流格式（通过 FFmpeg 可支持 MOV、M4A 等） 高质量录音（24bit/96kHz） 内置降噪、均衡器、压缩器、限制器等效果器 人声消除（Vocal Remover），利用相位抵消分离人声与伴奏 支持 VST2/VST3、LV2、Audio Units 插件 Nyquist 脚本：用 Lisp 方言编写自定义音频处理 适合谁：播客制作者、音乐爱好者、录音新手、偶尔修音的人。它是“音频里的记事本”——不华丽，但什么都能干一点。 官网： Ardour Ardour 是一款免费开源的数字音频工作站（DAW），功能对标 Pro Tools、Logic 等专业软件，支持 macOS、Windows 和 Linux。版本已迭代至 9.0。 核心功能： 录音与 MIDI 编曲：支持多通道同步录音（24 通道以上），任意数量的音轨和总线 非线性编辑：无损编辑，无限撤销/重做 专业级混音：浮点精度混音架构、发送与返送、自动化控制 插件格式全面：AudioUnit、LV2、VST2/VST3、LADSPA 高度灵活的信号路由：任意到任意的连接 与视频同步：采样级精确同步，适合电影/游戏音效制作 丰富的 MIDI 编辑功能（8.0 新增）：和弦编辑、量化、力度图等 Clip Launching 模式（7.0 新增）：类似 Ableton Live 的 loop 回放 系统要求：推荐 2GB 以上内存，安装约 600MB 空间。 适合谁：音乐制作人、播客重度用户、电影/游戏音效工作者、对音频有专业追求的人。学习曲线陡峭，但功能深度是 Audacity 无法比拟的。 官网： 15.5.4 对比与选择建议 | 软件 | 主要用途 | 复杂程度 | 对标付费软件 | 推荐人群 | |------|----------|----------|--------------|----------| | Clypra | 视频剪辑 | 中等 | 剪映（CapCut） | 短视频创作者、剪辑新手 | | Audacity | 音频编辑 / 录音 | 低 | Adobe Audition（基础部分） | 播客、录音、修音 | | Ardour | 全功能 DAW | 高 | Pro Tools、Logic | 音乐制作、专业混音 | 15.6 HDR 与色彩联动 从附录十四我们知道，Windows 的色彩管理比较麻烦。HDR 视频剪辑更是如此： HDR10：基础 HDR 标准，10-bit 色深，静态元数据。多数 HDR 显示器支持。 杜比视界（Dolby Vision）：更高级的标准，动态元数据（每帧亮度信息可不同），需要硬件和软件双端授权。 HLG：适合广播电视的 HDR 标准，无需元数据，兼容 SDR 显示器。 如果你对 HDR 视频剪辑有严肃需求，MacBook Pro 是目前最省心的选择（XDR 屏幕，峰值亮度 1600 尼特，系统级色彩管理）。在 Windows 下折腾 HDR 的时间成本可能远高于预期。 补充阅读 以下内容涉及 FFmpeg 命令行用法、I/P/B 帧深入原理、编码器调优和硬件检测。需要用到的时候再回来看。 主书里我还会涉及到 FFmpeg ，敬请期待 补充1：FFmpeg 命令行工具 FFmpeg 是一个开源的命令行音视频处理工具。几乎所有音视频软件的底层都用到了它。转格式、剪片段、压字幕，一行命令就能搞定。 安装 从 ffmpeg.org 下载 Windows 预编译包，解压后将 文件夹添加到系统 PATH。打开命令行输入 确认。 常用命令 格式转换： 视频裁剪（从 1 分 30 秒开始，裁 45 秒）： 参数说明： 起始时间， 持续时长， 不重新编码（直接拷贝流）。 放在 之前是快速搜索（基于关键帧），放在之后是精确搜索（逐帧解码）。 压制 HEVC（软件编码）： 使用 NVIDIA 显卡硬件编码（如果显卡支持）： 使用 Intel 核显硬件编码（如果核显支持）： 提取音频： 表示不要视频流， 表示音频码率。 下载 m3u8 视频（在线流媒体）： 批量处理 写一个简单的 Windows 批处理脚本（ ）： 更复杂的任务可以用 PowerShell 7 脚本（支持 并行处理）或 Python 调用 。FFmpeg 的强大之处在于：除去需要实时预览的调色等操作（其实也可以快速逐帧生成图片预览），其余的粗剪、转码、拼接、滤镜等，没有它干不了的。 补充2：I 帧、P 帧、B 帧的详细原理 视频压缩不存储每一帧完整画面，而是存储帧之间的“变化”。 I 帧（关键帧，Intra-frame）：完整存储一帧画面。体积最大，解码最快。视频里的“完整图像”。每间隔一定帧数就会出现一个 I 帧（由“关键帧间隔”参数控制）。 P 帧（前向预测帧，Predicted frame）：只存储和前一帧的差异。体积中等，解码时需要参考前面的 I 帧或 P 帧。 B 帧（双向预测帧，Bidirectional frame）：同时参考前一帧和后一帧，存储双向差异。体积最小，压缩率最高，但解码最慢。 为什么切在非 I 帧会花屏：P 帧和 B 帧只存了“变化”，没有完整画面。如果从 P 帧或 B 帧开始播放，解码器不知道前面是什么样子，只能猜测，画面上就会出现破碎的方块。所以在不重新编码的情况下裁剪视频，只能从 I 帧切。如果需要精确到任意帧的切割，必须重新编码。 补充3：编码器速度预设 x264/x265 的 参数从 到 ，越慢画质越好（同等码率下）。日常用 或 。 以上的收益已经很小。 ：编码极快，画质差，体积大 ：默认，平衡速度与质量 ：比 medium 慢约 50%，码率可节省 5%-10% ：很慢，收益递减 NVENC 的 有 （最快）到 （最慢，最好画质），默认 。 下画质有提升，但编码速度明显下降。 补充4：AV1 编码器对比 libaom-av1：AV1 的参考编码器，画质最好，但编码速度非常慢（编码 1 秒视频可能需几分钟到几十分钟）。 libsvtav1：英特尔主导开发的版本，编码速度快得多（比 libaom 快几百倍），画质也相当不错。日常压制 AV1 用 libsvtav1 即可。 补充5：2-pass 编码 第一遍分析视频，记录每一帧的复杂度；第二遍据此分配码率，在复杂场景给更多码率，简单场景给更少。适合需要精确控制输出文件大小的场景（例如上传网站有容量限制）。日常用 CRF 就够了，不需要二压。 补充6：杜比音频格式详情 AC-3：老一代杜比数字音频，DVD 时代的标准，5.1 声道，码率通常 448k 或 640k。 E-AC-3（Dolby Digital Plus）：杜比的有损环绕声，支持 5.1、7.1 声道，流媒体平台（Netflix、Disney+ 等）常用。码率通常 192k-768k。文件后缀可能是 。 TrueHD：杜比的无损环绕声格式，常见于蓝光原盘，体积大，需要 HDMI 或 eARC 才能直通。支持最多 7.1 声道。 补充7：硬件编码器支持检测 GitHub 上有 HwCodecDetect 工具，可以一键检测你的电脑支持哪些硬件编码器和解码器，以及它们能处理到多大分辨率。 它会输出一份报告，列明 NVENC、QSV、AMF、VAAPI、VideoToolbox 等各种接口的编码支持情况。 补充8：FFmpeg 流拷贝的坑 不重新编码，速度极快且无损。但裁剪视频时如果起始点不是 I 帧，FFmpeg 会从上一个 I 帧开始拷贝，导致你得到的片段开头比预期早了零点几秒。处理方法： 接受这个误差（通常误差在半秒以内，可以接受） 或者对开头几秒做重编码：先用 裁剪一个大范围，再用精确重编码裁剪头部 补充9：FFmpeg 滤镜链示例

title: 照片
content: 附录十六：照片 这个附录介绍摄影的一些基本概念——白平衡、ISO、快门速度、光圈、焦距、动态范围等，以及手机上的专业相机 App、RAW 格式的用处，还有简单的后期思路。哪怕你只是随手拍拍，多了解一点也没坏处。 16.1 曝光三要素：ISO、快门速度、光圈 一张照片的亮度，由三个东西共同决定：ISO（感光度）、快门速度、光圈。它们三个就像水龙头的三个阀门，一起控制流进相机的“水量”。 ISO（感光度） ISO 是相机传感器对光线的敏感程度。数值越小（如 ISO 100），对光越不敏感，画质越细腻、干净；数值越大（如 ISO 3200），对光越敏感，可以在很暗的环境下拍亮，但代价是画面会出现噪点（颗粒感）。 日常建议：光线好的时候用低 ISO（如 100-400），画质最好。光线暗的时候才考虑提高 ISO。 快门速度 快门速度是曝光的时间长度。快门越快（如 1/1000 秒），曝光时间越短，能“凝固”住运动中的物体（比如拍飞鸟、赛车）。快门越慢（如 1/30 秒或更慢），曝光时间越长，能拍出运动轨迹（比如夜晚车灯拉丝、流水雾化）。 安全快门：手持拍摄时，快门速度不要低于“等效焦距的倒数”。比如用 50mm 镜头，快门不要低于 1/50 秒，否则手抖会导致画面模糊。手机镜头等效焦距通常更短（约 24-28mm），安全快门大约在 1/30 秒左右。 光圈 光圈是镜头里开孔的大小，控制进光量，也影响景深（背景虚化程度）。 光圈越大（数值越小，如 F1.8），进光越多，背景越虚化。适合拍人像、特写。 光圈越小（数值越大，如 F8），进光越少，前景背景都清晰。适合拍风景、合影。 手机上的“光圈”：主流手机的摄像头光圈是固定的（无法调节）。手机上的“人像模式”不是靠调光圈，而是靠算法模拟虚化。所以你不需要在手机上纠结光圈参数，知道这个原理就行。 三个参数怎么配合 同样亮度的一张照片，可以有无数种参数组合。比如：大光圈 + 快快门 = 小光圈 + 慢快门。根据你的需要去取舍——想要背景虚化就用大光圈，想要拍清楚前后就用小光圈，想要定格瞬间就用快快门，想要拍光轨就用慢快门。 16.2 白平衡 白平衡（White Balance）的作用是让白色物体在照片里看起来是白色，而不被环境光源的颜色影响。 我们人眼很聪明，在黄色台灯下看白纸，大脑会自动把它“校正”成白色。但相机不会——如果不调白平衡，在黄光下拍白纸，照片里的白纸会偏黄。 相机通常有自动白平衡（AWB），大部分场景够用。但如果你发现照片整体偏黄或偏蓝，可以在拍摄时手动选择白平衡模式（日光、阴天、钨丝灯、荧光灯等），或者在后期软件（如 Lightroom）里调整色温滑块。 16.3 焦距与等效焦距 焦距（单位毫米，mm）决定画面能拍到多宽、物体能拉到多近。数值越小，视野越广（广角）；数值越大，视野越窄、拍得越远（长焦）。 超广角（14-24mm）：适合风景、建筑，视野宏大。 标准焦段（35-50mm）：接近人眼视角，适合街拍、人文。 长焦（70-200mm 以上）：适合拍远处的人、鸟、月亮。 等效焦距：手机和微单/单反的传感器尺寸不同，同样标注“24mm”，实际的视野范围不一样。为了方便比较，业界用“等效全画幅焦距”来统一标准。你不需要记公式，只要记住：手机主摄通常是等效 24-28mm 的广角，所谓的“长焦手机”可能是等效 70mm 或更长。 16.4 最近对焦距离 相机能拍多近的物体，是有极限的。如果你靠得太近，怎么按快门都对不上焦，这就是因为超过了“最近对焦距离”。 微距摄影（拍花蕊、昆虫）需要镜头支持很近的对焦距离。普通镜头的最近对焦距离通常是十几到几十厘米。如果你想用手机拍微距，可以留意手机是否有“微距模式”或“超级微距”，或者买一个外接微距镜头夹在摄像头上。 16.5 峰值对焦 峰值对焦 是手动对焦时的一个辅助功能。当你转动对焦环时，画面上合焦的区域会出现彩色颗粒（红色、黄色或白色），颜色最密集的地方就是最清晰的地方。 什么时候用：拍微距、拍星空、拍静物（比如产品摄影）时，自动对焦可能拉风箱或对不准，这时候切手动对焦，看着峰值提示拧到最清楚，比靠肉眼判断靠谱得多。大多数微单和部分手机的专业模式支持这个功能。 16.6 动态范围 动态范围 是相机能同时记录的最亮和最暗之间的范围。 高动态范围的场景：逆光拍人像——天空很亮，人脸很暗。如果相机动态范围不够，要么天空过曝（一片死白），要么人脸太暗（看不清五官）。 手机上的“HDR 模式”：就是通过连拍几张不同曝光的照片（一张亮部正常、一张暗部正常），再合成为一张亮部和暗部都清楚的照片。现在的计算摄影，很多手机默认就在后台跑 HDR，不需要你手动开。 什么时候会用到：拍日出日落、逆光人像、室内窗户边……凡是光比很大的场景，开 HDR 会有明显改善。 16.7 手机专业相机 App 手机自带的相机 App 通常把控制权藏得很深，只能点一下快门。如果你想要手动控制 ISO、快门、白平衡、对焦，并且拍摄 RAW 格式，可以装第三方相机 App。 iPhone 上：Halide Mark III Halide 是老牌的专业相机 App，最新版本是 Mark III。 支持手动控制所有参数（ISO、快门、白平衡、对焦） 可以拍摄 RAW（也支持 Process Zero 绕过苹果的自动处理） 新增了 Photo Lab 编辑器，可以编辑 RAW 照片 价格：不太了解，毕竟我没用过苹果。（但是有个朋友很常用halide） 安卓上：ProShot、Open Camera 安卓的开放性带来了更多的第三方相机 App。 ProShot：DSLR 风格的界面，手动控制 ISO、快门、白平衡、对焦，支持 RAW。被认为是安卓上最好的手动相机 App 之一。收费。 Open Camera：开源、免费、功能强大。支持手动控制、RAW、HDR、降噪等。如果你不想花钱，这款是最佳选择。完全够用。 Camera FV-5：也是一款经典的手动相机 App，支持长曝光、RAW，收费。 拍什么用这些 App：拍风景（手动对焦到无限远）、拍光轨（手动调慢快门）、拍 RAW 后后期……以及任何你想完全掌控照片的时候。 16.8 RAW 格式 16.8.1 RAW 是什么 手机和相机默认拍的是 JPG（或 HEIF），是经过相机内部处理的成品——白平衡、锐化、降噪、色彩风格都已经定死了，后期调整空间很小。 RAW 是传感器记录下来的原始数据。它保留了所有的亮度、颜色信息，没有被“处理”过。白平衡可以随意调、曝光可以拉回几档、阴影细节可以提亮——后期弹性非常大。 16.8.2 为什么 RAW 看起来灰灰的 刚拍出来的 RAW 照片，导入电脑或手机里看，通常是灰蒙蒙、低饱和度的。这是正常的。它不是“拍坏了”，是因为 RAW 没有经过相机内部的色彩和对比度处理。你需要用 Lightroom（LR）、Photoshop（PS）或其他能处理 RAW 的软件把它“冲”出来——调整曝光、对比度、饱和度、曲线等，这个过程叫“显影”。 16.8.3 手机的高像素和 RAW 现在手机动不动就标 48MP、64MP、108MP，但你拍出来的 RAW 很可能只有 12MP 或 16MP，这不是手机骗你——是传感器的工作方式决定的。 绝大多数高像素手机传感器采用 像素四合一（Quad Bayer） 或 十六合一 的设计。拍普通照片时，相邻的几个像素合并成一个大像素输出，获得更好的画质和进光量。一张 48MP 的传感器，四合一后输出的是 12MP。即使你拍摄 RAW，有的手机也只输出四合一的 RAW（比如 iPhone 的 ProRAW 默认是四合一的 12MP）——这不是坏事，四合一的 12MP RAW 画质通常比直接出 48MP 的 RAW 更好，因为单像素太小容易产生噪点。 如果你真的需要完整分辨率的 RAW（例如拍大幅打印），可以看看相机 App 里有没有“Full resolution RAW”或“Unbinned RAW”的选项。但大部分情况，四合一的 12MP RAW 已经够用了。 16.9 Raw vs JPG 直出 | 格式 | 文件大小 | 后期空间 | 适用场景 | |------|----------|----------|----------| | JPG / HEIF | 小 | 很小，调一下亮度还行，白平衡基本拉不回来 | 日常随手拍、发朋友圈、不打算修图 | | RAW | 很大 | 非常大，曝光可以拉回 ±2 档，白平衡随意调 | 拍了想精修、调色、打印、卖图 | 结论：随手拍拍用 JPG 够了；但如果你觉得这张照片将来“可能想修一修”，或者场景光比很大（逆光、夜景），顺手拍一张 RAW 存着——硬盘空间不值钱，错过了就拍不到了。 16.10 调色思路与工具 Lightroom（LR） Lightroom 是目前最主流、最好上手的照片后期软件。手机端、电脑端都有，订阅 Adobe 摄影计划（含 Photoshop）可得。手机版免费就可以用基础功能（调曝光、对比度、饱和度、曲线等）。 简单调色流程（以手机 LR 为例）： 导入 RAW（LR 会自动进入显影模式） 调整“亮度”区域的曝光、对比度、高光、阴影（把天空高光拉下来，把暗部细节提上去） 调整“颜色”区域的白平衡（色温、色调）、饱和度 套个预设或手动拉曲线（S 型曲线是增加对比度和通透感的简单方法） 最后适度加锐化和降噪（不要加过头） 两个提醒： 屏幕色彩要准：调了半天颜色，最后发现是自己的屏幕偏色，调出来的照片在别人手机上一片灰——这是很多新手都会踩的坑。如果你的电脑或手机屏幕偏冷或偏暖（和身边另一台设备对比一下），建议先在设置里关掉“动态色彩增强”、“鲜艳模式”等选项。最稳妥的是相信另一台已校准的设备（比如 iPad）或朋友的手机。 手机 LR 预设 ≠ 电脑 LR 预设：同一个预设文件，手机 LR 和电脑 LR 套出来的效果可能有差异——因为两端的色彩空间、渲染引擎不一样。所以如果你在手机上调好了一个预设，想拿到电脑上用，最好先对比一下，必要时微调。 各人有各人的风格 调色没有标准答案。有人喜欢高饱和浓郁风，有人喜欢低饱和清冷风，有人只调黑白。看你自己。多看（看别人的好照片，看色卡），多调（自己动手拉曲线、调 HSL），慢慢会形成自己的感觉。 补充阅读 以下内容涉及更深层的技术细节，需要时再回来看。 补充1：像素合并（Pixel Binning）的技术原理 Quad Bayer 排列的四合一传感器——四个同色像素以 2×2 阵列排列。日常拍摄时，四个像素合并成一个，输出较小分辨率的照片，但是每个“大像素”的感光面积相当于原来的四倍，信噪比更高。需要高分辨率时（如光线极好），可以解合并（Remosaic）输出全像素的 48MP 照片。部分手机还支持不同增益（ISO）的像素分别曝光再合成，以提升动态范围（单次曝光实现类似 HDR 的效果）。 补充2：白平衡更精细的调整 相机自动白平衡有时会被大面积单色（比如你站在一片红墙前面）骗到。如果发现拍出来的照片整体偏色，可以手动指定灰点：在 LR 等后期软件里，用白平衡吸管点击画面中本来应该是中性灰或白色的区域（比如水泥地、白墙、白纸），软件会自动校正全局色温。 补充3：动态范围与宽容度 “动态范围”是传感器能记录的最亮和最暗的光比。宽容度是 RAW 文件后期能把过曝或欠曝的区域拉回正常范围的能力。两者相关但不完全相同。高动态范围的传感器通常有高宽容度——你后期可以把暗部提亮 2-3 档而不出现明显噪点。 补充4：计算摄影对 RAW 的影响 现在手机的 RAW 已经和传统意义上的“纯 RAW”不太一样了。iPhone 的 ProRAW 在 RAW 数据基础上融入了 Deep Fusion 的多帧合成信息（已经叠了多张不同曝光的帧，在后台完成了 HDR 合并）。好处是同场景下 ProRAW 的宽容度远超普通 RAW；坏处是它已经带了一些“计算”痕迹，不是最原始的传感器数据。安卓厂商的“RAW”实现各异，有的也是多帧合成后的 DNG。所以如果你追求最原始的传感器输出，可能需要用第三方 App 且关闭所有多帧增强。 补充5：LR 调色的色彩空间设置 电脑版 LR 的工作空间默认通常是 ProPhoto RGB（很大），但导出给别人的照片建议转成 sRGB，这是最通用的色域，几乎所有屏幕都能正确显示。如果你在广色域屏幕上调完照片，导出时选了 ProPhoto RGB 或 Adobe RGB，发到微信或传到网页上，颜色会变灰。导出时记得选 sRGB。

title: VideoANDAudio
content: Appendix 15: Audio and Video This appendix introduces basic concepts and common tools for audio and video processing, including codecs, container formats, bitrate, OBS recording settings, and video editing software choices. The extended reading section covers FFmpeg command‑line usage and deeper technical concepts. 15.1 Codecs An encoder compresses raw audio or video data into a specific format. A decoder decompresses that data back into a playable signal. 15.1.1 Video Codecs | Name | Common encoders | One‑sentence explanation | |------|----------------|---------------------------| | H.264 / AVC | (software), (NVIDIA), (Intel) | Best compatibility – almost every device can play it. | | H.265 / HEVC | (software), (NVIDIA), (Intel) | Same quality as H.264 but smaller file size. | | AV1 | , (software) | Even higher compression, good for streaming. | Note: requires an NVIDIA GPU; requires an Intel iGPU. Not every computer has them. Software encoding vs. hardware encoding: Software encoding ( , , ): Better quality, smaller files, but uses the CPU heavily and is slow. Good for archiving and high‑quality encodes. Hardware encoding ( , ): Very fast (5‑10× faster than software), but slightly lower quality at the same bitrate. Good for screen recording, live streaming, and fast exports. 15.1.2 Audio Codecs | Name | Common encoder | One‑sentence explanation | |------|----------------|---------------------------| | AAC | | The most universal audio format today – almost every video uses it. | | MP3 | | Older format, good compatibility, but worse quality than AAC at the same bitrate. | | FLAC | | Lossless compression, large file size – good for archiving and listening to music. | | Opus | | Newer technology, excellent quality and compression; some older devices do not support it. | 15.2 Container Formats A container format is the "box" that holds video, audio, and subtitles. The same H.265 video can be put into an or into an . | Container | Characteristics | |-----------|-----------------| | MP4 | Most universal – almost every device plays it. Downside: usually can only hold one video track, one audio track, and one subtitle track. | | MKV | Very powerful – can hold multiple audio tracks, multiple subtitle tracks, and chapter information. If damaged, only the last few seconds are corrupted (the rest remains recoverable). | | MOV | Apple's QuickTime format, also supports multiple tracks. Good for exchanging files between Apple devices and Windows. | 15.3 Bitrate Bitrate is the amount of data used per second of video, measured in kbps (kilobits per second) or Mbps (megabits per second). Higher bitrate → better quality → larger file. CBR (Constant Bitrate) : The bitrate stays the same throughout. Suitable for live streaming. VBR (Variable Bitrate) : Simple scenes get a lower bitrate; complex scenes get a higher bitrate. Better quality at the same average bitrate. CRF (Constant Quality) : The encoder automatically allocates bitrate to keep the quality roughly constant for every frame. The most hassle‑free option for everyday encoding. 15.4 OBS Recording Settings 15.4.1 Basic Settings Output mode: Advanced → set output to "Output to file" Container format: Choose MKV (reason: if OBS crashes or your computer loses power during recording, MKV will only corrupt the last few seconds; MP4 will become completely unreadable) Encoder: If you have both an Intel iGPU and a discrete GPU → choose QuickSync HEVC (uses the iGPU to encode, does not compete with your games for GPU resources) If you have only an NVIDIA GPU → choose NVENC HEVC If you have only an AMD GPU → choose AMD AMF HEVC (good luck) 15.4.2 Recommended Settings | Resolution | Bitrate | Frame rate | Keyframe interval | B‑frames | |------------|---------|------------|-------------------|----------| | 1080p | 35 Mbps | 60 fps | 3 seconds | 3 | | 4K | 90 Mbps | 60 fps | 3 seconds | 3 | Games lack motion blur – every frame is a sharp instant capture. When the camera moves quickly, details can break up easily. Therefore, game recording requires higher bitrates than normal video. About B‑frames: B‑frames (bidirectional predicted frames) improve compression efficiency but increase encoding latency. Setting them to 3 is a good balance between quality and compatibility. 15.4.3 Administrator Privileges For some full‑screen games, if OBS cannot capture the game window, right‑click the OBS icon and select "Run as administrator". 15.5 Editing Software 15.5.1 Adobe Suite Premiere Pro: Video editing – one of the industry standards. After Effects: Visual effects, compositing, motion graphics. Audition: Audio editing, noise reduction, mixing. Adobe software is subscription‑based. You can download a trial version from Creative Cloud, then – without opening the software – immediately run Adobe GenP to activate it. I am not providing download links. Search GitHub or relevant forums for the steps. This touches on copyright issues, so please use your own judgement. 15.5.2 DaVinci Resolve A professional editing and color grading tool from Blackmagic Design. The free version is already extremely powerful – editing, color grading (used by Hollywood movies), Fairlight audio, and Fusion effects all integrated. If you care about color accuracy, this is often a better choice than Premiere. 15.5.3 Open‑Source Alternatives If you do not want to pay for software and do not want to deal with piracy, these three open‑source tools are worth trying. Clypra Clypra is a modern open‑source video editor built with Tauri, React, TypeScript, Rust, and FFmpeg, released under the MIT license. Its goal is to replicate the paid features of CapCut's international version for free. Because it does not use Electron (which consumes lots of memory), it starts faster and uses fewer resources than similar tools. Core features: Multi‑track professional timeline with drag‑and‑drop editing and frame‑level trimming Real‑time audio waveform display for easy beat‑matching Filmstrip preview for quick content navigation Text subtitles and titles with custom fonts Project management and auto‑save, with 100 levels of undo/redo Supports MP4, MOV, MKV, AVI (video) and MP3, WAV, AAC (audio) Cross‑platform: Windows, macOS, Linux Not yet implemented: AI auto‑subtitles, transition/effect libraries, colour grading, green screen keying (these are under development). Who it is for: Short‑form video creators, beginners, people who do not want to pay for CapCut. Basic editing is already usable. Website: Search GitHub for Audacity Audacity is a long‑established, easy‑to‑use open‑source multi‑track audio editor and recorder, released under GPLv3. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Core features: Multi‑track editing with unlimited tracks Import/export of WAV, AIFF, MP3, OGG, FLAC, and more (can support MOV, M4A, etc. via FFmpeg) High‑quality recording (up to 24‑bit / 96 kHz) Built‑in effects: noise reduction, EQ, compressor, limiter, and more Vocal remover (using phase cancellation to separate vocals from accompaniment) Supports VST2/VST3, LV2, and Audio Unit plugins Nyquist scripting for custom audio processing (using a Lisp dialect) Who it is for: Podcasters, music hobbyists, recording beginners, people who need occasional audio cleanup. It is the "Notepad of audio editors" – not fancy, but it can do a bit of everything. Website: Ardour Ardour is a free and open‑source digital audio workstation (DAW) that competes with Pro Tools, Logic, and other professional software. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux. The current version is 9.0. Core features: Recording and MIDI composition: multi‑channel simultaneous recording (24+ channels), unlimited tracks and busses Non‑linear editing: non‑destructive editing with unlimited undo/redo Professional mixing: floating‑point mixing architecture, sends and returns, automation Extensive plugin support: AudioUnit, LV2, VST2/VST3, LADSPA Highly flexible signal routing: any channel to any other channel Video sync: sample‑accurate synchronisation, suitable for film and game sound design Advanced MIDI editing (new in 8.0): chord editing, quantisation, velocity maps, etc. Clip Launching mode (new in 7.0): Ableton Live‑style loop playback System requirements: 2 GB RAM recommended, ~600 MB disk space. Who it is for: Music producers, heavy‑duty podcasters, film/game audio professionals, anyone who needs serious depth in audio. The learning curve is steep, but its depth is unmatched by Audacity. Website: 15.5.4 Comparison and Recommendations | Software | Main use | Complexity | Paid equivalent | Recommended for | |----------|----------|------------|-----------------|------------------| | Clypra | Video editing | Medium | CapCut | Short‑form creators, beginners | | Audacity | Audio editing / recording | Low | Adobe Audition (basic parts) | Podcasters, voice recording, quick fixes | | Ardour | Full‑featured DAW | High | Pro Tools, Logic | Music production, professional mixing | 15.6 HDR and Color Management (Recap) From Appendix 14, we know that color management on Windows is finicky. HDR video editing is even more so: HDR10: The baseline HDR standard, 10‑bit colour depth, static metadata. Supported by most HDR monitors. Dolby Vision: A more advanced standard with dynamic metadata (per‑frame brightness information). Requires licensing on both the hardware and software sides. HLG: An HDR standard for broadcast TV. No metadata needed and is backwards‑compatible with SDR displays. If you have serious HDR editing needs, a MacBook Pro is currently the most hassle‑free choice (XDR screen, 1600 nits peak brightness, system‑level colour management). The time cost of wrestling with HDR on Windows can far exceed your expectations. Extended Reading The following sections cover FFmpeg command‑line usage, the inner workings of I/P/B frames, encoder tuning, and hardware detection. Come back when you need them. I will cover FFmpeg in more depth in the main book – stay tuned. Extended 1: FFmpeg Command‑Line Tool FFmpeg is an open‑source command‑line audio and video processing tool. Almost every audio/video software uses it under the hood. Converting formats, cutting clips, burning in subtitles – all can be done with a single command. Installation Download the Windows pre‑built package from ffmpeg.org. Extract it, then add the folder to your system PATH. Open a command prompt and type to confirm it works. Common Commands Format conversion: Video cutting (start at 1 minute 30 seconds, take 45 seconds): Parameter explanation: start time, duration, do not re‑encode (copy the streams directly). Putting before performs a fast seek (based on keyframes); putting it after performs an accurate seek (decodes every frame). Encode to HEVC (software) : Use NVIDIA hardware encoding (if your GPU supports it): Use Intel iGPU hardware encoding (if your iGPU supports it): Extract audio: means "no video stream"; sets the audio bitrate. Download an m3u8 video (online stream) : Batch Processing Here is a simple Windows batch script ( ): For more complex tasks, use PowerShell 7 (which supports for parallel processing) or Python with . The power of FFmpeg is that – apart from tasks that require real‑time preview (e.g., colour grading) – almost everything else (rough cutting, transcoding, concatenation, filtering) can be done with it. Extended 2: I‑frames, P‑frames, B‑frames – Detailed Explanation Video compression does not store every frame as a full image. Instead, it stores the differences between frames. I‑frame (Intra‑frame) : Stores a complete frame. Largest size, fastest to decode. These are the "full images" in the video. An I‑frame appears every so often (controlled by the "keyframe interval" setting). P‑frame (Predicted frame) : Stores only the differences from the previous frame. Medium size. Decoding requires referring back to a previous I‑frame or P‑frame. B‑frame (Bidirectional frame) : Stores differences from both the previous frame and the next frame. Smallest size, highest compression, but slowest to decode. Why cutting at a non‑I‑frame causes corruption: P‑frames and B‑frames only store "changes", not full images. If playback starts at a P‑frame or B‑frame, the decoder does not know what the previous frame looked like, so it guesses – resulting in broken blocks on the screen. When cutting without re‑encoding, cuts can only be made at I‑frames. To cut at an arbitrary frame, re‑encoding is required. Extended 3: Encoder Speed Presets The parameter for x264/x265 ranges from to . Slower presets give better quality (at the same bitrate). For daily use, or is fine. Beyond , the gains are marginal. : Extremely fast encoding, low quality, large files : Default, balances speed and quality : About 50% slower than medium, saves 5‑10% bitrate : Very slow, diminishing returns For NVENC, the options range from (fastest) to (slowest, best quality). Default is . At , quality improves noticeably, but encoding speed drops significantly. Extended 4: AV1 Encoders Compared libaom-av1: The reference AV1 encoder. Best quality, but extremely slow (encoding 1 second of video can take minutes to tens of minutes). libsvtav1: Developed by Intel. Much faster (hundreds of times faster than libaom) and still delivers very good quality. For everyday AV1 encoding, use libsvtav1. Extended 5: 2‑pass Encoding The first pass analyses the video, recording the complexity of each frame. The second pass then allocates bitrate accordingly – giving more bits to complex scenes and fewer bits to simple scenes. This is useful when you need to hit an exact file size (e.g., a file size limit for uploading to a website). For daily use, CRF is sufficient; 2‑pass is not needed. Extended 6: Dolby Audio Formats – Details AC‑3: The older Dolby Digital audio format. The DVD era standard. Supports 5.1 channels, typical bitrate 448k or 640k. E-AC‑3 (Dolby Digital Plus) : Dolby's lossy surround sound format. Supports 5.1 and 7.1 channels. Commonly used by streaming platforms (Netflix, Disney+, etc.). Typical bitrate 192k–768k. File extension may be . TrueHD: Dolby's lossless surround sound format. Common on Blu‑ray discs. Large file size; requires HDMI or eARC for direct passthrough. Supports up to 7.1 channels. Extended 7: Hardware Encoder Support Detection There is a tool on GitHub called HwCodecDetect that detects which hardware encoders and decoders your computer supports, and up to what resolution. It produces a report listing support for NVENC, QSV, AMF, VAAPI, VideoToolbox, and other interfaces. Extended 8: Pitfalls of FFmpeg Stream Copy does not re‑encode – it is very fast and lossless. However, when cutting video, if the start point is not an I‑frame, FFmpeg will start copying from the previous I‑frame. This means the resulting clip will start a few hundred milliseconds earlier than you intended. How to handle this: Accept the small error (usually less than half a second, often acceptable) Or re‑encode just the beginning part: first cut a rough range with , then re‑encode the head section accurately Extended 9: FFmpeg Filter Chain Example

title: Photography
content: Appendix 16: Photography This appendix introduces basic photography concepts – white balance, ISO, shutter speed, aperture, focal length, dynamic range – as well as professional camera apps for phones, the usefulness of RAW format, and some simple post‑processing ideas. Even if you only take casual snapshots, a little extra knowledge never hurts. 16.1 The Exposure Triangle: ISO, Shutter Speed, Aperture The brightness of a photo is determined by three things: ISO (sensitivity), shutter speed, and aperture. They are like three valves on a water tap, together controlling how much light reaches the camera. ISO (sensitivity) ISO is how sensitive the camera sensor is to light. A lower number (e.g., ISO 100) means less sensitivity, cleaner and sharper image quality. A higher number (e.g., ISO 3200) means more sensitivity – you can take brighter photos in very dark conditions – but at the cost of noise (grain) appearing in the image. Everyday advice: Use low ISO (100–400) when light is good for the best quality. Only raise ISO when it is genuinely dark. Shutter speed Shutter speed is the duration of exposure. A fast shutter speed (e.g., 1/1000 second) freezes moving subjects (birds in flight, racing cars). A slow shutter speed (e.g., 1/30 second or slower) captures motion blur (light trails from cars at night, silky water). Safe shutter speed: When shooting handheld, do not go slower than roughly "1 / (equivalent focal length)". For a 50mm lens, stay above 1/50 second, otherwise camera shake will blur the photo. Phone lenses have shorter equivalent focal lengths (around 24–28mm), so a safe shutter speed is around 1/30 second. Aperture Aperture is the size of the opening in the lens. It controls how much light enters and also affects depth of field (background blur). Wide aperture (small number, e.g., f/1.8) → more light, more background blur. Good for portraits and close‑ups. Narrow aperture (large number, e.g., f/8) → less light, everything in focus. Good for landscapes and group photos. Aperture on phones: The main cameras on most phones have a fixed aperture – you cannot change it. The "portrait mode" on phones does not adjust aperture; it uses software to simulate blur. So you do not need to worry about aperture values on a phone – just understand the concept. How the three work together A photo with the same overall brightness can be taken with many different combinations of settings. For example: wide aperture + fast shutter speed = narrow aperture + slow shutter speed. Choose based on what you need – want background blur? Use a wide aperture. Want everything sharp? Use a narrow aperture. Want to freeze motion? Use a fast shutter speed. Want light trails? Use a slow shutter speed. 16.2 White Balance White balance (WB) makes sure that white objects look white in a photo, regardless of the colour of the light illuminating them. Our eyes are very clever: under a yellow desk lamp, we still see a white piece of paper as white – our brain automatically compensates. A camera does not. Without adjusting white balance, a photo of white paper taken under yellow light will look yellow-ish. Cameras usually have Auto White Balance (AWB), which works well in most situations. But if you find your photos looking too yellow or too blue, you can manually select a WB mode (daylight, cloudy, tungsten, fluorescent, etc.) when shooting, or adjust the temperature slider afterwards in software like Lightroom. 16.3 Focal Length and Equivalent Focal Length Focal length (measured in mm) determines how wide or zoomed‑in your view is. Smaller numbers → wider view (wide‑angle). Larger numbers → narrower view, bringing distant objects closer (telephoto). Ultra‑wide (14–24mm): landscapes, architecture – grand, sweeping views. Standard (35–50mm): roughly the field of view of the human eye – street photography, everyday scenes. Telephoto (70mm and above): distant subjects – birds, people, the moon. Equivalent focal length: Phone sensors and standalone camera sensors (mirrorless/DSLR) have different sizes. A lens marked "24mm" on a phone will show a different field of view than a 24mm lens on a full‑frame camera. To make comparisons easy, the industry uses "full‑frame equivalent focal length". You do not need to memorise the formula – just remember that a phone's main camera is typically around 24–28mm equivalent (wide‑angle), and what phone makers call "telephoto" might be around 70mm equivalent or longer. 16.4 Minimum Focus Distance Every lens has a limit to how close you can get to a subject and still focus. If you move too close, the camera will refuse to focus – you have exceeded the minimum focus distance. Macro photography (flower stamens, insects) requires a lens that can focus very close. Ordinary lenses have minimum focus distances of a few tens of centimetres. If you want to try macro on your phone, check if it has a "macro mode" or "super macro", or buy a clip‑on macro lens. 16.5 Focus Peaking Focus peaking is a manual focus aid. When you turn the focus ring, areas that are in focus are highlighted with coloured dots (red, yellow, or white). The densest area of dots is where the sharpest focus lies. When to use it: When shooting macro, starry skies, or still life (e.g., product photography), autofocus may hunt or miss. Switch to manual focus, turn the ring while watching the peaking overlay, and stop when the dots are brightest – much more reliable than relying on your eye alone. Most mirrorless cameras and some phone pro modes support this. 16.6 Dynamic Range Dynamic range is the range between the brightest and darkest parts that a camera can capture at the same time. A high‑dynamic‑range scene: a portrait against a bright sky. The sky is very bright, the face is much darker. If the camera's dynamic range is insufficient, either the sky will be blown out (pure white) or the face will be too dark (details lost). The "HDR mode" on phones does this: the camera takes several exposures in quick succession (one for the highlights, one for the shadows, etc.) and merges them into a single photo where both the bright sky and the dark face are visible. Modern computational photography often runs this process automatically in the background – you do not need to turn on an HDR switch. When to use it: Sunrises and sunsets, backlit portraits, scenes with bright windows and dark interiors – any time the contrast is very high, HDR (if not already automatic) will help significantly. 16.7 Professional Camera Apps for Phones The built‑in camera app on most phones hides most controls; you just press the shutter button. If you want manual control over ISO, shutter speed, white balance, and focus, and want to shoot RAW, install a third‑party camera app. On iPhone: Halide Mark III Halide is a well‑known professional camera app. The latest version is Mark III. Manual control over all parameters (ISO, shutter speed, white balance, focus) Can shoot RAW (also supports Process Zero, which bypasses Apple's automatic processing) Now includes a Photo Lab editor for editing RAW photos Price: I am not sure – I have never used an Apple device. (But a friend of mine uses Halide often.) On Android: ProShot, Open Camera Android's openness allows for more third‑party camera apps. ProShot: DSLR‑style interface, manual control over ISO, shutter speed, white balance, focus, RAW support. Considered one of the best manual camera apps on Android. Paid. Open Camera: Open source, free, powerful. Supports manual controls, RAW, HDR, noise reduction, and more. If you do not want to spend money, this is the best choice – completely sufficient. Camera FV‑5: Another classic manual camera app, supports long exposure and RAW. Paid. When to use these apps: Shooting landscapes (manual focus to infinity), capturing light trails (slow shutter speed manually), shooting RAW for later editing – any time you want full control over your photo. 16.8 RAW Format 16.8.1 What Is RAW? By default, phones and cameras save photos as JPG (or HEIF). These are finished products – white balance, sharpening, noise reduction, and colour style are all baked in. There is very little room for editing afterwards. RAW is the unprocessed data straight from the sensor. It retains all the brightness and colour information as it was captured, without any processing. White balance can be changed freely, exposure can be pulled back by several stops, shadow details can be brightened – the editing flexibility is enormous. 16.8.2 Why Does RAW Look Grey and Flat? When you first open a RAW photo on your computer or phone, it often looks greyish, low‑contrast, and desaturated. This is normal. It is not "broken". It is because the RAW file has not gone through the camera's internal colour and contrast processing. You need to use software like Lightroom, Photoshop, or another RAW processor to "develop" it – adjust exposure, contrast, saturation, curves, etc. This process is called demosaicing or developing. 16.8.3 High Megapixel Counts on Phones and RAW Phones today boast 48MP, 64MP, or even 108MP sensors, but the RAW you get is often only 12MP or 16MP. This is not the phone lying to you – it is how the sensors work. Most high‑megapixel phone sensors use Quad Bayer (or even 16‑cell) designs. In normal shooting, adjacent pixels are merged into larger "super‑pixels" to get better light capture and image quality. A 48MP sensor, when quad‑merged, outputs a 12MP photo. Even when you shoot RAW, many phones output the merged 12MP RAW (for example, iPhone's ProRAW defaults to 12MP from the merged output). This is not a bad thing – a 12MP merged RAW usually has better image quality than a full 48MP RAW, because individual pixels on a tiny sensor are very small and prone to noise. If you truly need full resolution RAW (e.g., for large prints), look in your camera app for an option like "Full resolution RAW" or "Unbinned RAW". But in most cases, the 12MP merged RAW is perfectly adequate. 16.9 RAW vs. Straight‑out‑of‑Camera JPG | Format | File size | Editing flexibility | Best for | |--------|-----------|---------------------|----------| | JPG / HEIF | Small | Very limited – small brightness adjustments maybe, but white balance is mostly fixed | Everyday snapshots, social media, when you do not plan to edit | | RAW | Large | Huge – exposure can be pulled ±2 stops, white balance can be changed freely | When you want to do serious editing, colour grading, printing, selling photos | Conclusion: For casual photos, JPG is fine. But if you think "I might want to edit this later", or if the scene has very high contrast (backlighting, night scenes), shoot a RAW copy as well – disk space is cheap, but a missed moment is gone forever. 16.10 Colour Grading – Ideas and Tools Lightroom (LR) Lightroom is the most mainstream and beginner‑friendly photo editing software. It is available on mobile and desktop. A Creative Cloud Photography plan (which includes Photoshop) gives you access. The mobile version's basic features (exposure, contrast, saturation, curves) are free. A simple editing workflow (using Lightroom mobile as an example) : Import the RAW (LR will automatically enter the "develop" mode) In the "Brightness" section, adjust exposure, contrast, highlights, and shadows (pull down the bright sky, lift the shadow details) In the "Colour" section, adjust white balance (temperature, tint) and saturation Apply a preset or manually adjust the curve (an S‑curve is a simple way to increase contrast and add "pop") Finally, add a little sharpening and noise reduction – do not overdo it Two important reminders: Your screen colour needs to be trustworthy: You spend time carefully adjusting colours, only to find that your own screen was off – and the photo looks completely different (often grey and flat) on someone else's phone. This is a classic beginner trap. If your computer or phone screen seems too warm or too cool (compare it with another device), go into its settings and turn off "vivid mode", "dynamic colour enhancement", or similar options. The safest approach is to trust a device you know is accurate (like an iPad) or a friend's phone. Mobile LR presets ≠ desktop LR presets: The same preset file can look different when applied in Lightroom mobile versus Lightroom desktop – because the two use different colour spaces and rendering engines. If you tweak a preset on your phone and want to use it on your computer, test it side‑by‑side first and be ready to make small adjustments. Everyone has their own style There is no single "correct" way to colour grade. Some people like rich, saturated, punchy colours. Others prefer muted, cool, desaturated tones. Some only work in black and white. It is up to you. Look a lot (at good photos, at colour charts), edit a lot (pull curves, adjust HSL sliders), and over time you will develop your own feel. Extended Reading The following sections go into deeper technical details. Come back when you need them. Extended 1: Technical Principle of Pixel Binning Quad Bayer sensors arrange four same‑colour pixels in a 2×2 array. In normal shooting, these four pixels are merged into one "super‑pixel", outputting a lower‑resolution image. However, each super‑pixel has four times the light‑gathering area of a single tiny pixel, resulting in much higher signal‑to‑noise ratio. When high resolution is genuinely needed (e.g., in excellent light), the sensor can perform a remosaic to output the full 48MP. Some phones also use different gain (ISO) levels on the different sub‑pixels and merge them later, improving dynamic range in a single shot (a kind of "HDR‑in‑one"). Extended 2: Fine‑tuning White Balance Auto white balance can be fooled by a scene dominated by a single colour (for example, if you stand in front of a large red wall). If your photos have a colour cast, you can manually set a grey point: in Lightroom or another RAW processor, use the white balance eyedropper to click on an area that should be neutral grey or white (e.g., a piece of concrete, a white wall, a white piece of paper). The software will correct the global colour temperature based on that sample. Extended 3: Dynamic Range vs. Latitude Dynamic range is the range between the brightest and darkest light levels that a sensor can capture in a single exposure. Latitude is how much you can later brighten underexposed areas or darken overexposed areas in a RAW file without introducing excessive noise or artefacts. They are related but not identical. A sensor with high dynamic range usually has good latitude – you can lift shadows by 2–3 stops without ruining the image. Extended 4: How Computational Photography Affects RAW Modern phones' RAW files are no longer "pure" RAW in the traditional sense. iPhone ProRAW, for example, starts with RAW data but then incorporates multi‑frame information from Deep Fusion (it has already merged several exposures at different brightness levels in the background). The benefit is that ProRAW's dynamic range in challenging scenes far exceeds what a traditional RAW would have. The cost is that it already carries some "computational" fingerprints – it is not the rawest of raw data. Android manufacturers' "RAW" implementations vary – some are also multi‑frame DNGs. If you truly want the most unprocessed sensor output, you may need to use a third‑party app and disable all multi‑frame enhancements. Extended 5: Colour Space Settings in Lightroom Lightroom's working space on the desktop is typically ProPhoto RGB (very large). However, for photos you export to share with others, you should convert to sRGB – the most universal colour gamut, which almost every screen can display correctly. If you edit a photo on a wide‑gamut screen, then export it as ProPhoto RGB or Adobe RGB and send it via WeChat or upload it to a website, the colours will appear dull and grey on most viewers' devices. Remember to select sRGB when exporting.

title: 安全
content: 附录十七：隐私与安全 这个附录介绍网络通信的基本原理（HTTPS、TCP、TLS）、密码管理器、两步验证（2FA），以及一些容易被忽视的隐私习惯。不深入技术细节，但会让你知道“数据在网线里是怎么跑的”以及“怎么防止自己的账号被别人拿走”。 17.1 数据在网线里是怎么跑的：TCP、TLS、HTTPS 当你打开一个网站（比如 ），背后发生了三件事：建立连接、加密通道、传输数据。 17.1.1 TCP：建立可靠的连接 TCP（Transmission Control Protocol，传输控制协议） 负责把数据可靠地从一端送到另一端。它会先把数据拆成一个个小包，每个包编号，发送出去，等对方确认收到了再发下一个。如果某个包丢了，TCP 会重发。 可以这样理解：TCP 像寄挂号信——每一封都有编号，收件人要签收，没收到就再寄一次。优点是可靠，缺点是慢一点（因为有来来回回的确认）。 和 UDP 的区别：UDP 像寄普通明信片——扔进邮筒就不管了，不确认对方是否收到。优点是快，缺点是可能丢包。视频通话、在线游戏常用 UDP（偶尔丢一帧画面还能忍，但延迟不能高）。 17.1.2 TLS：给数据上锁 TLS（Transport Layer Security，传输层安全协议） 是 HTTPS 里面那个“S”。它在 TCP 连接之上加了一层加密。你发送的数据在离开电脑之前被加密成密文，到达服务器后再解密。中间任何节点（路由器、运营商、Wi-Fi 热点）看到的都是乱码，无法读取内容。 TLS 的工作流程大致是： 你的电脑和服务器互相打招呼，协商加密算法 服务器出示数字证书（证明“我真的是百度”） 双方生成一个共同的会话密钥（只有你们两个知道） 之后的所有通信都用这个密钥加密 这就是为什么你在公共 Wi-Fi 里登录网银、输密码是相对安全的——数据是加密的，就算别人截获了也解不开。 17.1.3 HTTPS：HTTP + TLS HTTP（Hypertext Transfer Protocol，超文本传输协议） 是浏览器和服务器之间传输网页内容的协议。但 HTTP 是明文传输，别人可以偷看。HTTPS 就是 HTTP 加上 TLS 加密。 怎么看网站是不是 HTTPS：地址栏前面有一个小锁图标。点开它可以看证书信息。 17.2 密码管理 17.2.1 为什么需要密码管理器 大多数人所有网站用同一个密码。只要其中一个网站数据库泄露（这种事经常发生），黑客就会用这个密码去试你的邮箱、微信、支付宝——这叫“撞库”。 密码管理器可以帮你： 为每个网站生成随机强密码（比如 ） 自动填充登录框（不用记，也不用输） 同步到手机和电脑 17.2.2 Firefox 内置密码管理器 如果你用 Firefox 浏览器，自带的密码管理器就够用。 开启同步：注册 Firefox 账号，在设置里开启“同步”——密码、书签、历史会加密同步到你的其他设备（手机、另一台电脑）。 查看/管理密码：设置 → 隐私与安全 → 已保存的登录信息。可以在这里查看、删除、导出密码。 主密码（Master Password）：强烈建议设置一个“主密码”。Firefox 保存的密码默认是加密存储的，但只要你登录了 Windows，任何人打开 Firefox 就能看到你所有的密码。设置主密码后，每次打开 Firefox 或查看密码时需要输入一次主密码。路径：设置 → 隐私与安全 → 使用主密码。 缺点：Firefox 密码管理器只在 Firefox 浏览器里能用。如果你用其他浏览器或手机 App，它就帮不上忙了。 17.2.3 跨平台密码管理器 如果你需要跨浏览器、跨 App，可以试试： Bitwarden：开源、免费（高级版每年 10 美元）。支持 Windows、macOS、Linux、iOS、Android，浏览器插件全覆盖。可以自己搭建服务器（不推荐小白做）。这是目前个人用户最稳妥的选择。 KeePass：纯本地存储，数据库文件放自己手里。功能强大但界面老气。需要手动同步数据库文件（用网盘）。 1Password：收费。你可以读这一篇博客 , ta写的很好。 17.2.4 绝对不能做的事 ❌ 把密码写在便利贴上贴显示器 ❌ 在微信/QQ里发密码截图 ❌ 用“记住密码”功能但不设主密码（谁都能看你电脑） ❌ 所有网站用同一个密码 17.3 两步验证（2FA） 17.3.1 什么是 2FA 2FA（Two-Factor Authentication，双因素认证） 是在密码之外再加一层保护。登录时除了输密码，还要输入一个动态生成的 6 位数字验证码（通常 30 秒变一次）。即使别人偷了你的密码，没有这个验证码也登不上。 常用的 2FA 是 TOTP（Time-based One-Time Password，基于时间的一次性密码）。原理：你和服务器共享一个密钥，基于当前时间生成一个 6 位数字。因为时间不会骗人，双方算出来的数字一样。 17.3.2 微软验证器（Microsoft Authenticator） 微软验证器是比较好用的 2FA 工具之一。手机端免费，支持云备份（需要微软账号）。 重要：换机前必须先解除 2FA 关联 这是很多人在换手机时踩过的大坑。 假设你用微软验证器绑定了好几个账号——Google、GitHub、Steam、你的学校邮箱。你买了一部新 iPhone，用苹果的“一键换机”把数据迁移过去。迁移完成后，微软验证器也会被拷过来，但是那些 2FA 密钥不会跟着迁移。因为 TOTP 的密钥存储方式特殊，简单的“复制 App 数据”不包含密钥。 更麻烦的是：如果你的多个账号是互相绑定的——比如你登录 Google 需要 GitHub 验证码，登录 GitHub 需要 Google 验证码——换机后两边都登不上去，形成一个闭环。 正确做法： 在换机之前，登录每一个绑定了 2FA 的网站 进入账户安全设置，把 2FA 关掉（或者“删除此设备”） 确认所有账号都解除绑定后，再换新手机 新手机到手，重新安装微软验证器 一个一个重新绑定 2FA（扫描二维码或手动输入密钥） 如果已经换完了怎么办： 大部分网站会提供“备用恢复码”——在你开启 2FA 时，网站会给你一组成串的字符，让你抄下来或打印出来。用恢复码可以登录进去，然后重新绑定。 如果你连恢复码都丢了，只能联系网站客服，提交身份证明（身份证、手持证件照片等），等对方帮你解绑。这个过程可能需要几天甚至几周。 所以在开启任何 2FA 时，恢复码一定要存好（打印出来，或者存到不是这台手机的地方）。 17.3.3 哪些账号值得开 2FA 邮箱：你的 Gmail、Outlook、学校邮箱——因为很多网站用“忘记密码”往邮箱发重置链接。邮箱被攻破等于所有账号失守。 Apple ID / Google 账号 / 微软账号：这些是你手机的钥匙。 Steam：游戏库存值钱，Steam 被盗找回很麻烦。 GitHub：如果你是计算机专业学生，代码仓库被删或被人塞恶意代码，后果严重。 密码管理器：Bitwarden、1Password 等支持 2FA，建议开启。 不建议开的：那些你几乎不登录、丢了也无所谓的小论坛账号。 17.3.4 2FA 的备份方案 除了微软验证器，还有几个选择： 2FAS：开源，支持 iOS/Android，有云备份（通过 iCloud/Google Drive），界面清爽。推荐。 Aegis（仅安卓）：开源，支持备份到本地文件（加密后存到网盘），功能强大。 17.4 几个容易被忽略的隐私习惯 17.4.1 浏览器不要保存银行卡信息 Chrome/Edge 会问你是否保存信用卡信息以便下次自动填充。方便是方便，但谁打开了你的浏览器（或者你电脑被远程控制），就能看到你的完整卡号、有效期、甚至 CVV 码（部分版本）。 建议：不保存。自己输 16 位卡号也没多慢。 17.4.2 公共 Wi-Fi 咖啡馆、机场、酒店的公共 Wi-Fi 可能是钓鱼热点（别人架一个叫“Starbucks Wi-Fi”的假热点）。你连上去后，对方可以抓包你的 HTTP 流量。 保护措施： 尽量避免在公共 Wi-Fi 上输密码 如果一定要用，尽量访问 HTTPS 网站（小锁图标是绿的） 最安全的是用手机热点，或者挂自己的代理/VPN 17.4.3 屏幕锁 很多人没有设置电脑的屏幕锁（Windows 按 锁屏）。在宿舍、实验室、图书馆，你走开接个水，别人就能坐你电脑前看你微信、邮件、论文。 建议： Windows：设置 → 账户 → 登录选项 → 添加 PIN 或密码 养成习惯：人离开，按 补充阅读 以下内容涉及 HTTPS 证书、TLS 握手细节和密码学基础概念，难度较高。用到了再回来看。 补充1：数字证书与 CA HTTPS 里的证书由 CA（Certificate Authority，证书颁发机构） 签发。你的操作系统和浏览器内置了一组受信任的 CA 根证书（如 DigiCert、Let's Encrypt、GlobalSign）。当你访问 时，服务器会出示一张证书，浏览器检查证书是否由某个受信任的 CA 签发、证书上的域名是否和正在访问的域名一致、证书是否过期。全部通过才会建立 TLS 连接。这也解释了为什么“下载未知来源的根证书”是危险行为——一旦安装了一个恶意 CA 证书，攻击者就可以伪造任何网站的证书，你的浏览器还会显示“安全”。 补充2：TLS 1.2 与 TLS 1.3 的区别 TLS 1.3 比 1.2 快一个往返时间（RTT）。TLS 1.2 需要两次握手（约 2 RTT）才能开始传输数据；TLS 1.3 简化了握手过程（1 RTT，甚至 0 RTT 恢复会话）。安全性也更高——移除了一些过时的加密算法（如 RSA 密钥交换、CBC 模式），强制使用前向保密（Forward Secrecy）的密钥交换算法。目前主流浏览器和服务器都已支持 TLS 1.3。 补充3：密码管理器加密原理 密码管理器存储的密码数据库是加密的（AES-256）。解密密钥由你的主密码派生而来。主密码不会存储在任何服务器上——Bitwarden、1Password 等采用零知识架构：服务器只存储加密后的数据块，没有你的主密码，他们自己也无法解密你的密码库。这也是为什么“忘记主密码”通常是不可恢复的——没有任何“找回密码”按钮。 补充4：TOTP 的时间同步问题 TOTP 依赖设备时间准确。如果你的手机时间比标准时间偏差超过 30 秒，生成的验证码会无效。手机开启“自动设置时间”通常没问题。如果发现验证码总是输错，去设置里校准时间。离线设备（如硬件令牌）也有内部的电池时钟，年头长了会漂移，需要重新同步。 补充5：恢复码的存储 开启 2FA 时网站给的恢复码（通常是 8-10 个单词或一串数字）是用来救命的。存储建议： 打印出来放在钱包里（不推荐放在电脑桌面） 保存在密码管理器里（Bitwarden 支持存储 2FA 恢复码的笔记） 保存在加密的笔记 App 里（如 Standard Notes、Joplin） 不要存在手机相册里（手机丢了就全丢） 补充6：钓鱼网站与 HTTPS 误区 HTTPS ≠ 网站可信。钓鱼网站也可以免费申请到 Let's Encrypt 的证书，地址栏照样有小锁图标。看到小锁只说明“你和这个网站的通信是加密的”，不代表“这个网站是合法的”。判断方法：检查域名拼写（ 还是 ），看是不是和你平时访问的一模一样。

title: SSH和内网穿透
content: 附录十八：SSH 与内网穿透 这个附录介绍 SSH 是什么、怎么用，以及当你的电脑没有公网 IP 时，怎么从外面访问它（内网穿透）。不深入原理。 主要作用是防止你对如何连上学校机房跑仿真一头雾水。 18.1 SSH 是什么 SSH（Secure Shell，安全外壳协议） 是一种加密的网络协议，用于安全地远程登录另一台电脑。 为什么需要 SSH：以前人们用 telnet 远程登录，但 telnet 所有数据（包括密码）都是明文传输。谁在中间一抓包，你的密码就没了。SSH 把整个通信过程加密了，中间的人看到的是一堆乱码。 SSH 能干什么： 远程登录服务器（取代 telnet） 安全传输文件（SFTP、SCP） 隧道转发（把其他不安全协议的流量塞进 SSH 加密通道） 跑远程命令（ ） 大学里什么时候会用上： 连接学校实验室的 Linux 服务器做作业、跑实验 连接学校提供的计算集群（超算中心） 连接树莓派、NAS 等设备 从宿舍连接实验室的电脑（配合内网穿透） 18.2 SSH 和其他协议的区别 | 协议 | 加密 | 典型用途 | |------|------|----------| | Telnet | 明文 | 老式远程登录（现在已经不推荐用了） | | SSH | 加密 | 远程命令行、文件传输 | | RDP | 加密 | Windows 远程桌面（图形界面） | | VNC | 可选 | 远程桌面，默认不加密 | | VPN | 加密 | 整个网络流量都走隧道 | | HTTP | 明文 | 网站 | | HTTPS | 加密 | 网站（加密版） | 简单记：命令行远程用 SSH，图形界面 Windows 远程桌面用 RDP，整台电脑的网络都走隧道用 VPN。 18.3 Windows 自带的 OpenSSH Windows 10/11 已经内置了 OpenSSH 客户端，不需要装 PuTTY 之类的第三方软件。 检查是否已安装：设置 → 系统 → 可选功能 → 搜索“OpenSSH 客户端”。没有的话点“添加功能”。 基本用法（在 CMD、PowerShell 或 Windows Terminal 里）： 第一次连接时，会提示你确认服务器的指纹（公钥）。输入 回车，之后就不会再问了。 常用参数： 指定端口（默认 22） 指定私钥文件（免密登录用） 退出 SSH 连接：输入 或按 。 18.4 免密登录（SSH 密钥） 输密码太麻烦，而且自动化脚本需要人输密码。可以配免密登录。 在本地电脑生成密钥对： 一路回车（建议设置一个密码保护私钥）。会在 目录下生成两个文件： ：私钥（别给别人） ：公钥（放到服务器上） 把公钥上传到服务器： 输一次密码后，以后连接就不用再输了。 为什么用 ed25519：比 RSA 更快、更安全、密钥更短。老系统可能不认识，那就用 。 18.5 别名与配置文件 连多台服务器，每次输入 很烦人。可以在 里配别名。 示例内容： 之后只需要 就能连上了。 18.6 内网穿透：没有公网 IP 怎么办 大多数家庭宽带没有公网 IPv4 地址。大学里的实验室、宿舍网络通常也是内网——你的电脑没有独立的公网 IP，外面的人直接连不上你。 什么是内网穿透：内网穿透（NAT traversal）是指让外网能够访问内网设备的技术。原理是你的电脑主动连上一个有公网 IP 的服务器（中转站），外面的人通过这个服务器访问你的电脑。 大学场景举例： 你在宿舍，想从外面（家里、实验室、实习公司）连回宿舍电脑拿文件 你在实验室，想从宿舍连回实验室的服务器跑代码 你做了一个网页，想临时给同学看看，但不想买服务器 FRP 是目前最流行的自建穿透工具。开源免费，Go 语言写的，支持 TCP、UDP、HTTP、HTTPS。但需要自己有一台有公网 IP 的服务器（VPS）来搭服务端。 如果不想自己买服务器，可以用公共服务。推荐两个： Openfrp：有免费套餐（限速 12 Mbps，隧道数 2），支持 TCP/UDP/TLS/HTTPS。适合游戏联机、远程桌面、网站临时测试。 cpolar（极点云）：功能强大，场景适配广，支持 HTTP/HTTPS/TCP。免费版每日更换域名，适合临时调试。 其他公共服务（Ngrok、Natapp、SAKURA FRP 等）也可以，开箱即用，不需要自己有服务器。 注意：国内公共服务很多要求实名认证，要花钱，这是合规要求。 18.7 大学实验室的 SSH 跳板机 很多学校的实验室或超算中心不允许直接公网 SSH 登录，而是需要先登录一台跳板机（Jump Server / Bastion Host），再从跳板机登录内网的服务器。 典型流程： （跳板机） 在跳板机上 （内网服务器） 嫌两步麻烦，可以在 里配置 ： 之后直接 就可以一步登入实验室服务器。 18.8 小结 | 场景 | 推荐方案 | |------|----------| | 服务器远程管理 | SSH 密钥免密登录 + config 别名 | | 同局域网内的电脑互访 | 直接用 SSH 内网 IP | | 从外网访问没有公网 IP 的设备 | openfrp / cpolar / FRP 自建 | | Windows 远程桌面（图形界面） | SSH 隧道转发 RDP，或直接用内网穿透工具转发 3389 端口 | | 大学跳板机 | config 配置 ProxyJump | SSH 本身功能远不止于此，还支持端口转发、代理跳转等高级用法。不过对日常使用来说，学会 、配好免密登录、知道内网穿透怎么搞，已经够用了。

title: 远程传输
content: 附录十九：远程传输 这个附录介绍手机和电脑之间传文件的方法。不用数据线，不用看手机文件管理里乱七八糟的文件夹，几种方式各取所需。 19.1 为什么传个文件这么麻烦 手机和电脑之间传文件，常见的方法各有各的烦： 微信/QQ：要压缩画质，大文件不让传，还得登录同一个账号 数据线：要找线，插上还要选模式，手机文件管理里一堆看不懂的文件夹名 蓝牙：慢，容易断 网盘：要先上传再下载，绕远路，限速 其实有更好的办法。下面按推荐程度排序。 19.2 Snapdrop：最省事的方案 Snapdrop 是一个网页版的局域网传输工具。不需要安装任何软件，不需要登录账号，只要手机和电脑连在同一个 Wi-Fi 下，打开浏览器就能传。 怎么用： 手机和电脑连同一个 Wi-Fi 手机和电脑都打开浏览器，访问 页面会自动发现同一网络下的其他设备，显示为圆形图标 点击对方的图标，选择文件，对方点击“保存”即可接收 优点： 什么都不用装，打开网页就能用 文件不经过任何服务器，只在设备之间点对点传输，安全 支持任何设备（iPhone 用 Safari，安卓用 Chrome，电脑用 Edge 都行） 缺点： 必须在同一个 Wi-Fi 下（不能跨网络） 单文件太大可能会慢，建议 100MB 以内 一句话：临时传几张照片、一个小文档，Snapdrop 最快。 19.3 KDE Connect：功能最全的方案 KDE Connect 是一个开源的全能型跨设备通信工具。原本是 Linux 上的 KDE 桌面环境的配套工具，现在已经支持 Windows、macOS、Android、iOS 。 除了传文件还能干什么： 手机和电脑共享剪贴板（手机上复制，电脑上 Ctrl+V 粘贴） 手机通知同步到电脑（电脑上查看微信消息，不用拿手机） 手机当电脑遥控器（控制音乐播放、PPT 翻页） 找手机（让手机响铃） 设备间双向传文件 安装方法： Windows：Microsoft Store 搜索“KDE Connect”安装 Android：Google Play 或 F-Droid 搜索“KDE Connect” iOS：App Store 搜索“KDE Connect” 电脑端不需要登录任何账号，手机和电脑在同一个 Wi-Fi 下就能配对 配对步骤： 手机和电脑连同一个 Wi-Fi 打开两边的 KDE Connect，手机会自动发现电脑 点击“配对”，电脑上确认 一句话：如果你经常在手机和电脑之间切换工作，装了 KDE Connect 会爽很多。 19.4 共享文件夹（SMB） Snapdrop 和 KDE Connect 都需要两边都操作（一个发、一个收）。如果你只是想“在手机上随时翻电脑里的文件”，最好的办法是在电脑上开一个共享文件夹，手机当网络硬盘挂载。 电脑端设置（Windows）： 右键要共享的文件夹 → 属性 → 共享 → 高级共享 勾选“共享此文件夹”，权限里添加 或 ，给“读取”权限 记下电脑的局域网 IP：Win+R 输入 ，再输入 ，找“IPv4 地址”（如 ） 手机端访问： 安卓：推荐用 CX 文件管理器（Play 商店或官网下载） 打开 CX → 网络 → 远程存储 → SMB 输入电脑 IP（如 ），用户名和密码（如果电脑设了的话） 连上后就能直接浏览电脑里的文件，像操作本地文件一样 iOS：用自带的“文件”App 就够了 打开“文件”App → 右上角 → 连接服务器 输入 （注意是 开头） 输入电脑的用户名和密码（Windows 登录账号） 连上后共享文件夹会出现在“共享”列表里 优点： 一次配好，以后随时能用 手机可以直接看电脑里的视频、文档，不用先下载 支持多台设备同时访问 缺点： 只有局域网能用（离开 Wi-Fi 范围就连不上了） 19.5 FTP / HTTP 文件服务器 如果你只是偶尔从手机下载电脑上的文件，不需要反过来上传，可以在电脑上开一个临时的 HTTP 或 FTP 服务器。手机上用浏览器就能访问。 Windows 快速开 HTTP 服务器（不装软件）： 在要共享的文件夹里，在地址栏输入 回车 输入 （需要装 Python） 手机上浏览器访问 ，就能看到文件夹里的文件列表，点击直接下载 用 FTP（适合需要上传）： 下载一个小巧的 FTP 服务器软件（如 Quick'n Easy FTP Server），5 分钟配好 手机用 CX 文件管理器或浏览器（ ）连接 19.6 总结 简单选择： 临时传文件 → Snapdrop 想深度打通手机和电脑 → KDE Connect 想随时访问电脑上的所有文件 → 开共享文件夹 + CX/iOS 文件 以上所有方法都不走互联网（在同一个 Wi-Fi 下），不消耗流量，也不用担心隐私泄露。离开家/宿舍就没法用了——那是内网穿透的事，附录十八讲过了。

title: 总结
content: 附录二十：总结 实践的部分基本都讲完了。主书会涉及更底层的东西和代码，后续的附录会涉及一些个人化的分享，放在单独的文件夹里。 书时进终语 余既冠而临此界兮，启重匣以晨光。 键纵横其若阡陌兮，屏浩渺其如八荒。 初举手而犹疑兮，恐一触而迷方。 幸有人兮告余以周行，曰： “彼内核非虎兕兮，虽深藏而可量。 彼协议非天网兮，虽错综而可详。 彼脚本非符咒兮，虽玄奥而可彰。 唯忘机而习之兮，自能通其玄黄。” 余乃涉文件之渊薮兮，凿分区以为仓。 树千枝于D盘兮，标数字以成章。 遇乱码而弗惊兮，知编码之可匡。 逢报错而弗惧兮，解日志而循墙。 游网络之浩渺兮，窥七层之脊梁。 译NAT之幽微兮，度防火墙之津梁。 设代理以驰骋兮，破壁垒而望四方。 调Clash之经纬兮，择节点以分流光。 观编码之流变兮，识264之短长。 析AV1之精微兮，辨容器之宫商。 架OBS以录天光兮，调码率以御奔浪。 用FFmpeg而万化兮，粗剪于指掌。 有数门焉曰开源兮，抱薪火以相传。 有群贤兮默默，铸基石而弗言。 有协议焉守自由兮，虽分叉而同源。 有镜站焉汇百川兮，供学子以取泉。 有尺素焉曰Markdown兮，脱重裘而著轻裳。 有神器焉曰Git兮，录毫厘于宇内而囊八荒。 有密语曰SSH兮，越山海以启远程之窗。 有奇术曰穿透兮，入内网而会高堂。 嗟夫！ 余初入此匣如入暗室兮，今秉烛而识其方。 向之惧者今为器兮，向之惑者今为常。 非余智之有过人兮，积跬步以致遐疆。 非天工之独厚余兮，假AI以为舟航。 乱曰： 筑金屋兮贮数据，穿云网兮游无方。 调光影兮悦心目，录时序兮惜流光。 非极乐兮实有用，非捷径兮阻且长。 已启程兮莫回首，越此域兮见新阳。 昔见万卷皆无字兮，今信笔以书丹。

title: Security
content: Appendix 17: Privacy and Security This appendix introduces the basic principles of network communication (HTTPS, TCP, TLS), password managers, two‑factor authentication (2FA), and some easily overlooked privacy habits. It does not go deep into technical details, but it will help you understand "how data travels through the network" and "how to prevent your accounts from being stolen." 17.1 How Data Travels Through the Network: TCP, TLS, HTTPS When you open a website (for example, ), three things happen behind the scenes: a connection is established, an encrypted channel is created, and data is transmitted. 17.1.1 TCP: Establishing a Reliable Connection TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is responsible for delivering data reliably from one end to the other. It first breaks the data into small packets, numbers each packet, sends them out, and waits for an acknowledgement before sending the next. If a packet is lost, TCP resends it. Think of it this way: TCP is like sending a registered letter – each letter has a tracking number, the recipient must sign for it, and if it is lost, you send another copy. The advantage is reliability; the downside is that it is slower because of all the back‑and‑forth acknowledgements. The difference from UDP: UDP is like sending a postcard – you drop it in the mailbox and forget about it, with no confirmation of receipt. The advantage is speed; the downside is that packets may be lost. Video calls and online games often use UDP (losing an occasional frame is tolerable, but high latency is not). 17.1.2 TLS: Locking the Data TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the "S" in HTTPS. It adds an encryption layer on top of the TCP connection. The data you send is encrypted into ciphertext before it leaves your computer and is only decrypted when it reaches the server. Any intermediate node (router, ISP, Wi‑Fi hotspot) sees only gibberish and cannot read the content. The TLS handshake works roughly like this: Your computer and the server greet each other and agree on an encryption algorithm. The server presents a digital certificate (to prove "I really am Baidu"). Both sides generate a shared session key (known only to the two of you). All subsequent communication is encrypted with that key. This is why it is relatively safe to log into your online banking or type passwords on public Wi‑Fi – the data is encrypted, so even if someone intercepts it, they cannot decrypt it. 17.1.3 HTTPS: HTTP + TLS HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the protocol browsers and servers use to transmit web page content. However, HTTP transmits everything in plain text, meaning anyone can eavesdrop. HTTPS is HTTP with TLS encryption. How to tell if a website uses HTTPS: There is a small padlock icon next to the address bar. Click on it to see the certificate information. 17.2 Password Management 17.2.1 Why You Need a Password Manager Most people use the same password for every website. If just one of those websites has a database breach (which happens often), hackers will try that password on your email, WeChat, Alipay – a technique called credential stuffing. A password manager helps you: Generate a strong, random password for each website (e.g., ) Automatically fill in login forms (no need to remember or type) Sync your passwords across your phone and computer 17.2.2 Firefox Built‑in Password Manager If you use Firefox, its built‑in password manager is sufficient for many people. Enable sync: Register for a Firefox account, then turn on sync in the settings – your passwords, bookmarks, and history will be synced (encrypted) to your other devices (phone, another computer). View / manage passwords: Settings → Privacy & Security → Saved Logins. Here you can view, delete, or export your passwords. Master Password: It is strongly recommended to set a Master Password. By default, Firefox saves your passwords encrypted, but if you are logged into Windows, anyone who opens Firefox can see all your saved passwords. Setting a Master Password means you will need to enter it once per session when opening Firefox or viewing passwords. Path: Settings → Privacy & Security → Use a Master Password. Downside: The Firefox password manager only works inside the Firefox browser. If you use other browsers or mobile apps, it cannot help you. 17.2.3 Cross‑Platform Password Managers If you need something that works across browsers and apps, consider these: Bitwarden: Open source, free (premium is $10 per year). Supports Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, and has browser extensions for everything. You can also self‑host (not recommended for beginners). This is currently the safest choice for individual users. KeePass: Local storage only – the database file stays on your own machine. Very powerful, but the interface looks dated. You need to sync the database file manually (e.g., using cloud storage). 1Password: Paid. You can read this blog post – it is very well written. 17.2.4 Things You Must Never Do ❌ Write your passwords on a sticky note and attach it to your monitor. ❌ Send password screenshots over WeChat or QQ. ❌ Use "remember password" in your browser without also setting a Master Password (anyone who sits down at your computer can see them). ❌ Use the same password for every website. 17.3 Two‑Factor Authentication (2FA) 17.3.1 What Is 2FA? 2FA (Two‑Factor Authentication) adds an extra layer of protection on top of your password. When you log in, besides entering your password, you also need to enter a dynamically generated 6‑digit verification code (usually changing every 30 seconds). Even if someone steals your password, they cannot log in without that code. The most common form of 2FA is TOTP (Time‑based One‑Time Password) . The principle is: you and the server share a secret key, and you both generate a 6‑digit number based on the current time. Because time does not lie, both sides calculate the same number. 17.3.2 Microsoft Authenticator Microsoft Authenticator is one of the better 2FA tools. It is free on mobile phones and supports cloud backup (requires a Microsoft account). Important: You must remove 2FA associations before switching phones This is a big trap many people fall into when they change phones. Suppose you have used Microsoft Authenticator to set up 2FA for several accounts – Google, GitHub, Steam, your university email. You buy a new iPhone and use Apple's "quick transfer" to migrate your data. After the migration, Microsoft Authenticator is copied over, but the 2FA secrets are not migrated. TOTP secrets are stored in a special way that a simple "copy app data" does not include them. To make matters worse, if your accounts are cross‑dependent – for example, you need a GitHub code to log into Google, and a Google code to log into GitHub – after switching phones you cannot log into either, creating a loop. The correct procedure: Before switching phones, log into every website that has 2FA enabled. Go to the account security settings and turn off 2FA (or "remove this device"). Confirm that all accounts have been disassociated, then set up your new phone. On the new phone, reinstall Microsoft Authenticator. Re‑enable 2FA for each account one by one (scan the QR code or manually enter the secret key). What if you have already switched phones? : Most websites provide recovery codes – when you first enabled 2FA, the site gave you a set of codes or words to write down or print. Use one of those recovery codes to log in, then re‑bind the 2FA. If you have lost the recovery codes as well, you must contact the website's customer support, prove your identity (ID card, photo holding your ID, etc.), and wait for them to remove 2FA for you. This process can take days or even weeks. Therefore, whenever you enable 2FA on any account, store the recovery codes safely (print them out, or save them somewhere other than that phone). 17.3.3 Which Accounts Are Worth Enabling 2FA On? Email: Your Gmail, Outlook, school email – because many sites send password reset links to your email. If your email is compromised, all your other accounts are at risk. Apple ID / Google account / Microsoft account: These are the keys to your phone. Steam: Your game library has real value, and recovering a stolen Steam account is a pain. GitHub: If you are a computer science student, your code repositories could be deleted or malicious code could be inserted – the consequences are severe. Password manager: Bitwarden, 1Password, etc. – if they support 2FA, enable it. Not recommended: Small forum accounts that you almost never log into and would not care about if lost. 17.3.4 Backup Options for 2FA Aside from Microsoft Authenticator, here are a few other choices: 2FAS: Open source, supports iOS/Android, has cloud backup (via iCloud/Google Drive), clean interface. Recommended.
