Aegis (Android only): Open source, supports backup to a local file (encrypted and then stored in cloud storage), very powerful. 17.4 Some Easily Overlooked Privacy Habits 17.4.1 Do Not Let Your Browser Save Credit Card Information Chrome/Edge will ask if you want to save your credit card information for auto‑fill later. It is convenient, but if someone opens your browser (or if your computer is remotely controlled), they can see your full card number, expiration date, and even the CVV (in some versions). Suggestion: Do not save it. Typing 16 digits yourself is not that slow. 17.4.2 Public Wi‑Fi Public Wi‑Fi in coffee shops, airports, and hotels can be malicious hotspots (someone sets up a fake hotspot named "Starbucks Wi-Fi"). Once you connect, they can capture your HTTP traffic. Protection measures: Avoid typing passwords on public Wi‑Fi whenever possible. If you must use it, try to visit only HTTPS websites (the padlock icon will be green). The safest approach is to use your phone's hotspot or connect through your own proxy/VPN. 17.4.3 Screen Lock Many people do not set a screen lock on their computer (in Windows, press to lock). In a dormitory, lab, or library, you walk away for a minute to get water, and someone else can sit down at your computer and read your WeChat, email, or thesis draft. Suggestions: Windows: Settings → Accounts → Sign‑in options → add a PIN or password. Develop the habit: when you step away, press . Extended Reading The following sections cover HTTPS certificates, TLS handshake details, and some fundamental cryptographic concepts. They are more advanced. Come back when you need them. Extended 1: Digital Certificates and Certificate Authorities The certificates used in HTTPS are issued by a CA (Certificate Authority) . Your operating system and browser come with a built‑in set of trusted CA root certificates (e.g., DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, GlobalSign). When you visit , the server presents a certificate. The browser checks whether the certificate was issued by a trusted CA, whether the domain name on the certificate matches the domain you are visiting, and whether the certificate has expired. Only if all checks pass will the browser establish a TLS connection. This also explains why "downloading a root certificate from an unknown source" is dangerous – once you install a malicious CA certificate, an attacker can forge valid certificates for any website, and your browser will show it as "secure". Extended 2: TLS 1.2 vs. TLS 1.3 TLS 1.3 is faster by one round trip (RTT). TLS 1.2 requires two handshakes (about 2 RTT) before it can start transmitting data. TLS 1.3 streamlines the handshake (1 RTT, and even 0 RTT for session resumption). It is also more secure – it removes outdated cryptographic algorithms (such as RSA key exchange and CBC mode) and requires Forward Secrecy for key exchange. Most mainstream browsers and servers now support TLS 1.3. Extended 3: How Password Managers Encrypt Data The password database stored by a password manager is encrypted (typically using AES‑256). The decryption key is derived from your master password. The master password is never stored on any server – services like Bitwarden and 1Password use a zero‑knowledge architecture: the server stores only the encrypted data blob; without your master password, even they cannot decrypt your vault. This is also why "forgetting your master password" is usually unrecoverable – there is no "forgot password" button. Extended 4: Time Synchronisation Issues with TOTP TOTP relies on your device having an accurate clock. If your phone's time is off by more than 30 seconds from the standard time, the generated codes will be invalid. Enabling "auto‑set time" on your phone usually avoids this problem. If you find your codes are consistently rejected, go to your device settings and calibrate the time. Offline devices (e.g., hardware tokens) also have internal battery‑powered clocks that drift over the years and may need to be resynchronised. Extended 5: Storing Recovery Codes The recovery codes (usually 8‑10 words or a string of numbers) that a website gives you when you enable 2FA are lifesavers. Storage recommendations: Print them out and keep them in your wallet (not recommended to store them on your computer desktop). Store them in your password manager (Bitwarden allows notes for 2FA recovery codes). Store them in an encrypted notes app (e.g., Standard Notes, Joplin). Do not store them in your phone's photo gallery (if your phone is lost, everything is lost). Extended 6: Phishing Sites and the HTTPS Misconception HTTPS ≠ the website is trustworthy. Phishing sites can also obtain a free Let's Encrypt certificate and show a padlock icon in the address bar. Seeing a padlock only tells you that "communication with this website is encrypted", not that "this website is legitimate". How to tell: check the domain name spelling – is it or ? Make sure it is exactly the same domain you always use.

title: SSHandNATTraversal
content: Appendix 18: SSH and NAT Traversal (Intranet Penetration) This appendix explains what SSH is, how to use it, and how to access your computer from outside when it does not have a public IP address (often called "intranet penetration" or "NAT traversal"). It does not go deep into theory. The main goal is to prevent you from being completely lost when you need to connect to your university's computing lab to run simulations. 18.1 What Is SSH? SSH (Secure Shell) is an encrypted network protocol used to securely log into another computer remotely. Why SSH is needed: In the past, people used telnet for remote login. However, telnet sends all data (including passwords) in plain text. Anyone who can capture network traffic in the middle can steal your password. SSH encrypts the entire communication – anyone in the middle sees only gibberish. What SSH can do: Log into a remote server (replacing telnet) Securely transfer files (SFTP, SCP) Forward tunnels (push traffic from other, less secure protocols through an encrypted SSH channel) Run remote commands ( ) When you might use SSH at university: Connecting to your department's Linux server to do assignments or run experiments Connecting to a university computing cluster (supercomputing centre) Connecting to a Raspberry Pi, NAS, or other device on your lab network Connecting from your dormitory to a lab computer (often combined with NAT traversal) 18.2 How SSH Differs from Other Protocols | Protocol | Encryption | Typical use | |----------|------------|--------------| | Telnet | Plain text | Old‑style remote login (no longer recommended) | | SSH | Encrypted | Remote command line, file transfer | | RDP | Encrypted | Windows Remote Desktop (graphical interface) | | VNC | Optional | Remote desktop – not encrypted by default | | VPN | Encrypted | Whole network traffic goes through a tunnel | | HTTP | Plain text | Websites | | HTTPS | Encrypted | Websites (encrypted version) | Quick summary: For command‑line remote access, use SSH. For a graphical Windows desktop, use RDP. To tunnel all network traffic from your whole computer, use a VPN. 18.3 Windows Built‑in OpenSSH Windows 10 and 11 come with an OpenSSH client built in. You do not need to install third‑party software like PuTTY. Check if it is installed: Settings → System → Optional features → search for "OpenSSH Client". If it is not there, click "Add a feature". Basic usage (in CMD, PowerShell, or Windows Terminal): The first time you connect, you will be prompted to confirm the server's fingerprint (its public key). Type and press Enter – after that, you will not be asked again. Common parameters: to specify a port (default is 22) to specify a private key file (used for passwordless login) To exit an SSH session: Type or press . 18.4 Passwordless Login (SSH Keys) Typing a password every time is annoying, and automation scripts cannot easily handle interactive password entry. You can set up passwordless login. Generate a key pair on your local computer: Press Enter all the way through (it is a good idea to set a password to protect your private key). This creates two files in the directory: : your private key (never share this) : your public key (this goes on the server) Upload the public key to the server: After entering your password once, subsequent connections will not require a password. Why ed25519? It is faster, more secure, and uses shorter keys than RSA. Some older systems may not recognise it – in that case, use . 18.5 Aliases and the SSH Config File If you connect to several servers, typing every time is tedious. You can set up aliases in . Example content: After that, you only need to type to connect. 18.6 NAT Traversal (Intranet Penetration): What If You Have No Public IP? Most home broadband connections do not have a public IPv4 address. University lab and dormitory networks are typically the same – your computer does not have a standalone public IP, so people from outside cannot connect directly to you. What is NAT traversal? NAT traversal (often called "intranet penetration") refers to techniques that allow external networks to access devices on an internal network. The principle is that your computer actively connects to a server that does have a public IP (a relay). Outside users then reach your computer through that relay server. University scenarios: You are in your dorm and want to connect back to your dorm computer from outside (home, the lab, your internship company) to retrieve files. You are in the lab and want to connect from your dorm to the lab server to run code. You have created a simple webpage and want to temporarily show it to classmates, but you do not want to buy a server. FRP is currently the most popular self‑hosted tunnelling tool. It is open source, free, written in Go, and supports TCP, UDP, HTTP, and HTTPS. However, you need your own server with a public IP (a VPS) to run the FRP server component. If you do not want to buy your own server, you can use public services. Two recommendations: Openfrp: Has a free tier (speed‑limited to 12 Mbps, 2 tunnels). Supports TCP/UDP/TLS/HTTPS. Suitable for game hosting, remote desktop, temporary website testing. cpolar: Feature‑rich and well‑suited for many scenarios. Supports HTTP/HTTPS/TCP. The free tier provides a domain name that changes daily – good for temporary debugging. Other public services (Ngrok, Natapp, SAKURA FRP, etc.) are also available – they work out of the box without requiring your own server. Note: Most domestic public services require real‑name verification. This is a compliance requirement. 18.7 University Lab SSH Jump Servers Many university labs or supercomputing centres do not allow direct public SSH logins. Instead, you must first log into a jump server (bastion host) , and from there log into the internal lab server. Typical workflow: (jump server) On the jump server, (internal lab server) If you find two steps annoying, you can configure in your : After that, typing logs you directly into the lab server in one step. 18.8 Summary | Scenario | Recommended solution | |----------|----------------------| | Remote server management | SSH key‑based passwordless login + config aliases | | Access between computers on the same local network | Direct SSH using the internal IP address | | Access a device without a public IP from outside | Openfrp / cpolar / self‑hosted FRP | | Windows Remote Desktop (graphical) | Forward RDP through an SSH tunnel, or directly forward port 3389 using a NAT traversal tool | | University jump server | Use in your SSH config | SSH is capable of far more – port forwarding, proxy jumping, and other advanced features. However, for daily use, knowing , setting up passwordless login, and understanding how to do NAT traversal is already enough.

title: RemoteTransfer
content: Appendix 19: Remote File Transfer (Between Phone and Computer) This appendix introduces several ways to transfer files between a phone and a computer. No data cables, no hunting through confusing folder names in your phone's file manager. Pick the method that suits your needs. 19.1 Why Is Transferring Files So Annoying? Common methods for transferring files between a phone and a computer each have their own frustrations: WeChat / QQ: Compresses images, blocks large files, and you must be logged into the same account on both devices. USB cable: You have to find the cable, plug it in, select the right mode on the phone, and then dig through a bunch of folders with cryptic names. Bluetooth: Slow and prone to disconnecting. Cloud storage: You upload first, then download – a long detour, often with speed limits. There are better ways. The methods below are ordered by how strongly they are recommended. 19.2 Snapdrop: The Most Hassle‑Free Option Snapdrop is a web‑based local network file transfer tool. No software installation required, no login needed. As long as your phone and computer are on the same Wi‑Fi network, you can transfer files by opening a browser. How to use: Connect both your phone and computer to the same Wi‑Fi network. On both devices, open a browser and go to . The page automatically discovers other devices on the same network, showing them as circular icons. Tap the icon of the target device, select a file, and on the receiving device click "Save" to accept. Advantages: Nothing to install – just open a webpage. Files do not pass through any server; they are transferred directly between devices (peer‑to‑peer), so it is secure. Works on any device (Safari on iPhone, Chrome on Android, Edge on Windows – all fine). Disadvantages: Both devices must be on the same Wi‑Fi network (cannot work across different networks). Very large files may be slow – it is best for files under 100 MB. In one sentence: For quickly transferring a few photos or a small document, Snapdrop is the fastest. 19.3 KDE Connect: The Most Feature‑Rich Option KDE Connect is an open‑source, all‑purpose cross‑device communication tool. Originally developed for the KDE desktop environment on Linux, it now supports Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS. What it can do besides file transfer: Share clipboard between phone and computer (copy on your phone, paste on your computer with Ctrl+V). Sync phone notifications to your computer (read WeChat messages on your PC without picking up your phone). Use your phone as a remote control for your computer (control music playback, flip through PowerPoint slides). Find your phone (make it ring). Bidirectional file transfer. Installation: Windows: Search the Microsoft Store for "KDE Connect". Android: Search Google Play or F‑Droid for "KDE Connect". iOS: Search the App Store for "KDE Connect". No login required on the computer side. As long as the phone and computer are on the same Wi‑Fi, they can pair. Pairing steps: Connect both devices to the same Wi‑Fi network. Open KDE Connect on both devices. The phone should automatically discover the computer. Tap "Pair" and confirm on the computer. In one sentence: If you frequently switch between working on your phone and your computer, installing KDE Connect will make your life much smoother. 19.4 Shared Folder (SMB) Snapdrop and KDE Connect both require action on both ends (one sends, one receives). If you simply want to "browse files on my computer from my phone at any time", the best approach is to set up a shared folder on your computer and mount it as a network drive on your phone. Setting up on the computer (Windows) : Right‑click the folder you want to share → Properties → Sharing → Advanced Sharing. Check "Share this folder". In the permissions, add or and give "Read" permission. Note down your computer's local IP address: press , type , then type . Look for the "IPv4 Address" (e.g., ). Accessing from your phone: Android: Recommended app: CX File Explorer (from Google Play or the official website). Open CX File Explorer → Network → Remote Storage → SMB. Enter your computer's IP address (e.g., ) and your Windows username/password if required. Once connected, you can browse files on your computer just like local files. iOS: The built‑in "Files" app is sufficient. Open the "Files" app → tap the (three dots) at the top‑right → Connect to Server. Enter (note the prefix). Enter your Windows username and password (the same credentials you use to log into Windows). After connecting, the shared folder appears under "Shared". Advantages: Set it up once, and it is always available. You can directly watch videos or open documents from your computer on your phone – no need to download them first. Multiple devices can access the same shared folder simultaneously. Disadvantages: Only works on the local network (you cannot use it when away from your Wi‑Fi). 19.5 Temporary HTTP / FTP File Server If you only occasionally need to download files from your computer to your phone (and never upload), you can start a temporary HTTP or FTP server on your computer. Your phone can then access it through a browser. Quick HTTP server on Windows (no extra software) : Open the folder you want to share. In the address bar, type and press Enter. In the command prompt, type (requires Python to be installed). On your phone, open a browser and go to . You will see a file listing; tap any file to download it. Using FTP (better if you need to upload as well): Download a small FTP server application (e.g., Quick'n Easy FTP Server). It takes about 5 minutes to set up. On your phone, connect using CX File Explorer or a browser ( ). 19.6 Summary Simple choice: For a one‑off file transfer → use Snapdrop. If you want to deeply integrate your phone and computer → use KDE Connect. If you want to always have access to all files on your computer from your phone → set up a shared folder + CX File Explorer (Android) or the Files app (iOS). All of the methods above stay within your local network (same Wi‑Fi). They do not consume mobile data and do not raise privacy concerns. Once you leave your home or dorm, they will no longer work – but that is a NAT traversal problem, covered in Appendix 18.

title: Conclusion
content: Appendix 20: Conclusion The practical parts are mostly finished. The main book will cover lower‑level topics and code, and later appendices will include some personal sharing, placed in a separate folder. A Closing Poem I remember the first time I opened this machine. The keys were a field of unknown furrows. The screen, a blank ocean. My finger hovered — afraid that one wrong touch would send me wandering forever. Then someone told me a simple thing: Nothing inside is a tiger. No protocol is a net you cannot untie. No script is a spell — only a language waiting to be read. Press on. You'll find your way. So I did. I learned to carve my own folders from the wild disk, to name each branch so I could find it again. When the screen spat out gibberish, I learned it was just a missing map. When an error flashed red, I learned to ask the logs — and they answered, quietly, like old walls giving up a hidden door. I walked into the network. Seven layers of invisible silk. NAT, firewall, proxy — each a gate, not a wall. I learned to set my own path across the ocean, to let my packets choose their own currents. Clash in the background, a quiet compass. I learned how light becomes numbers. H.264, AV1, containers, codecs. OBS to catch the passing sky. FFmpeg in my palm — a knife that cuts any shape. And then I found the great invisible city — open source. Millions of hands passing fire. No one asks your name. They only ask: can you carry this forward? I learned the licenses, the forks that return to the same river. I found the mirrors where every stream gathers, so a student anywhere can drink. I learned Markdown — to write without heavy armour. Git — to track every heartbeat of my work, from one machine to every corner of the earth. SSH — a whisper that crosses mountains and opens a window on a distant desktop. And tunnelling — to slip through the back ways and sit down at the great table inside. Now I understand. When I first entered this box, I was standing in a dark room. Now I carry my own candle. What I feared, I use. What confused me has become my daily bread. I am not wiser than others. I only put one foot down, then another. And I am not alone — there is something else now, a quiet companion I can ask: AI, show me the way. Alas! So here is my short creed: I will build a house of gold for my data. I will walk through every cloud without a map. I will bend light and shadow until they please my eye. I will carve time itself into small, saved moments. This is not paradise. It is work. It is not a shortcut. It is long, and sometimes hard. But I have already begun. I will not look back — except to see you. Beyond this field, I see a new sun. And when you step onto the same path, I will already be there, hand outstretched. — A fellow traveller, who once stood where you stand, and now walks ahead — but never so far that I cannot turn back, take your hand, and say: you can do this too.
